The review covers how key heavy metals poison the body and the health effects that follow. Exposure comes from polluted water, soil, air, and some work settings. Damage can hit the nerves, kidneys, and other organs over time. Gathering the mechanisms in one place helps doctors spot metal poisoning and helps officials set safer limits.

The team analyzed data from tens of millions of individuals to assess trends in obesity and overweight prevalence and the burden they cause. The authors estimate how common these diseases are, how many deaths they cause, and how much healthy life they take away, country by country. Their results show a heavy and uneven burden that falls hardest where smoking, air pollution, and limited care combine. Because anyone qualified can use the same data, studies based on it can be checked and repeated, and the dataset has become a training ground for clinical data science.

Joint resolutions carry the force of law when passed by both chambers and signed. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
europmc-pmc7880217: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on problems and advances (new steps forward) in clinical (in patients) uses of stromal cells. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
plaw-115-11-2017: This 2017 joint resolution disapproving the rule submitted by the Department of Defense, the General Services Administration, and the National Aeronautics and Space Admin. Joint resolutions carry the force of law when passed by both chambers and signed. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
europmc-pmc7203417: Yan and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on phytoremediation: a promising approach for revegetation of heavy metal-polluted land. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8728817: This 2022 research paper covers tumor-the tissue surrounding a tumor-responsive nanomedicine (ultra-small-particle medicine) for boosted cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system). The past decades have witnessed great progress in cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system), which has profoundly revolutionized. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8459317: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on deciphering osteoarthritis genetics across 826,690 individuals from 9 groups. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9381717: Doctors and scientists took on a new gene set identifies senescent cells and helps predict senescence-linked pathways across tissues in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc8491217: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at lipid metabolism (how cells turn food into energy) in cancer progression (worsening) and treatment plans. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9029217: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at antimicrobial (germ-killing) action of quercetin: an approach to its mechanistic principle. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9038417: Doctors and scientists took on global increase in breast cancer incidence (new cases): risk factors and preventive measures in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc7809617: A fresh look at progression (worsening) of myopia in school-aged children after COVID-19 home confinement arrived with this 2021 research paper. Importance time spent in outdoor activities has lowered owing to home confinement. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
plaw-115-13-2017: In 2017, Congress used this joint resolution to overturn a federal agency rule. Under the Congressional Review Act, Congress can reject recently finalized rules with a majority vote and the president's signature. The rule is then treated as if it never took effect.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-317: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at state and Local Governments: Growing Fiscal Challenges Will Emerge during the Next 10 Years. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-617: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on tax Compliance: Businesses Owe Billions in Federal Payroll Taxes. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
europmc-pmc7441617: A 2020 review paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at consumption of ultra-processed foods and health results: a systematic review (a review of every study) of epidemiological studies. It pulls together all the available studies on the question and grades the evidence. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
plaw-115-10-2017: This 2017 law, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Transition Authorization Act, approves national Aeronautics and Space Administration Transition programs and spending levels. Authorization laws set policy and funding ceilings; other spending laws provide the actual money. It stands as Public Law 115-10 of the 115th Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-517: The Government Accountability Office dug into nursing Homes: Federal Monitoring Surveys Demonstrate Continued Understatement of Serious Care Problems and CMS Oversight Weaknesses in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
the-merry-wives-of-windsor-pg1517: Falstaff's schemes collapse in this edition of Shakespeare's Windsor farce: the two merry wives compare his identical love letters and plot a delicious revenge. Duckings in the Thames, beatings in disguise, and a midnight fairy prank complete his humiliation. Pure comic mischief, written for laughs alone.
the-queen-of-hearts-pg1917: Wilkie Collins's 1859 story collection: ten tales told by ten guests, from mysteries to adventures. Varied, entertaining, and full of his narrative tricks, it shows his range beyond the big novels. A fine sampler of his shorter fiction.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume seventeen: old Fritz, the lonely last years, the king outliving his age. Carlyle's hero in winter, still working, still defiant. The most moving section of the vast work, as the thunder quiets. The old king's loneliness is the most human part of Carlyle's epic.
the-skin-game-a-tragi-comedy-pg2917: John Galsworthy's 1920 Skin Game: old gentry versus new money. The tragi-comedy of class war, sharp and balanced. A stage triumph. Old land, new money, bitter comedy, galsworthy's class war on stage, Galsworthy's class war on stage.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-17: The seventeenth volume offers more fruits of Montaigne's tower. He reflects on travel, change, and the self that endures through all. The voice is intimate, unhurried, and wise. Four hundred years have not dimmed its charm.
plos-pone-0329717:
Benoit Paquette led a team of eight authors studying an unwanted side effect of radiotherapy, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Radiation treats triple-negative breast cancer, but plasma taken from patients during treatment can spur cancer cells to invade more. The team traced that effect to a protein called Rab4A.

Paquette's group showed that Rab4A helps drive the rise in invasion caused by treatment-time plasma. Blocking it could stop therapy from backfiring on the patients it aims to save. The finding is early, from cell work, but it names a precise point of intervention. It also warns clinicians that blood-borne signals during radiotherapy deserve study, not only the tumor under the beam.
plos-pone-0355417:
Ameen Chaudry led a team of eight authors taking stock of diversity in orthopaedic surgery, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Orthopaedics remains one of the least diverse specialties in medicine. The team examined residency applications to ask where diversity currently stands in the pipeline that feeds the field.

Chaudry's numbers show how far the pipeline has come and how far it still has to go. Application data reveal whether diversity efforts fail at attracting applicants or at selecting among them, two very different problems. A specialty that treats patients of every background benefits when its surgeons reflect that range. Honest stocktaking is the precondition for programs that aim to widen the door.
plos-pone-0356617:
Amina Mouhamed, Jim Al-Khalili, and Marco Sacchi published a 2026 theoretical study in PLOS ONE on a quantum puzzle at the heart of psychiatry's oldest drug. Lithium has steadied bipolar disorder for decades, yet nobody knows exactly how it works. Its two isotopes have different nuclear spins, and some studies hint they act differently in biology. They ask whether lithium's spin could steer a radical pair mechanism, a quantum effect where magnetism changes chemical outcomes, in a pairing of flavin with the vitamin C radical.

Using density functional calculations and spin simulations, they model how lithium's nuclear spin might shift the balance of reaction products from these fleeting radical pairs. The vitamin C radical is a plausible partner because it is plentiful in the brain and long-lived. Whether such spin effects matter in patients is unproven, the authors stress, but the calculations make the idea concrete enough to test.
plos-pone-0357117:
Philipp Naß and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for PRIMA, a German project turning ordinary GP practices into multiprofessional care centers. Germany's primary care is strained by aging patients, chronic disease, and workforce shortages. The model adds specially trained nurses to practice teams. It gives them extended duties and reorganizes who does what inside the practice. Triage software can be added, and chronically ill high-risk patients are the focus.

The evaluation compares patients in twenty intervention practices against matched controls from routine insurance claims, over twelve months. The main measure is how many emergencies occur that good ambulatory care should have prevented. Healthcare use, deaths, continuity, and costs are also tracked. A parallel study follows how the change actually unfolds in daily work. The aim is to show whether nurse-integrated practices deliver better, more productive care, evidence German health policy lacks.
plos-pone-0357917:
Hui G. Cheng and coauthors published a 2026 longitudinal study in PLOS ONE following Americans through a cancer diagnosis to map how health, habits, and finances change together. Using fifteen waves of a national retirement study spanning three decades, they identified several thousand newly diagnosed people, matched each to similar cancer-free controls, and aligned timelines to the diagnosis year.

Diagnosis hit like a step down: self-rated health dropped sharply and functional limits jumped, with only partial recovery afterward. Depressive symptoms spiked and stayed elevated for years, and physical activity stayed suppressed even longer. Some changes were welcome: smoking fell at diagnosis and stayed lower, while weight and drinking shifts faded. Work and money suffered too: employment dropped and out-of-pocket spending jumped by over two thousand dollars a year. Survivorship care, they say, should plan for this whole bundle, not just the tumor.
plos-pone-0356917:
Marika A. de Hoop-Sommen and coauthors published a 2026 modeling study in PLOS ONE supporting guidelines for a delicate switch in children's intensive care. A child is moved from continuous morphine or fentanyl to methadone, then tapered away to prevent withdrawal. Clinicians lack agreed conversion ratios and taper speeds. The team built physiology-based models of how children's bodies handle all three drugs, checked them against published data, and simulated many plans.

The simulations pointed to clear working ratios: a fentanyl-to-methadone ratio of one to ten and a morphine ratio of one to one kept methadone in the therapeutic range. Most published tapering schedules peaked at similar methadone levels, except the gentlest low-risk schedules of two protocols. An expert panel of pediatric intensivists and pharmacists turned the results into recommendations. The models support, rather than replace, bedside judgment.
plos-pone-0354517:
Rebekah Sullivan, Andrew Gardiner, and Glen Cousquer study health care for homeless people in the United Kingdom who live with companion dogs. About one in ten people seeking shelter own an animal, most often a dog, and that bond can block access to housing and clinics. Their 2026 paper uses deep interviews with homeless dog owners and with health, vet, and housing staff.

Both sides described human and animal health as tangled together, not separate problems. Joint clinics at one site drew interest but also raised worries about space and safety. Sullivan and colleagues favor a looser goal: coordinated care across services that respects the pair as a unit. They argue that ignoring the dog often means losing the person too.
plos-pone-0348517:
Nouh Mounadi and co-authors screen plant compounds in simulation as possible blockers of two respiratory viruses at once: influenza A and a lesser-known cousin that also causes severe chest illness. Approved drugs exist for flu but options stay thin overall. The team docked known antiviral plant compounds against one key protein from each virus, then checked the best fits for drug-like behavior, stability in motion, and binding strength.

Dozens of compounds docked well against both targets, scoring better than the reference drugs used for comparison. A handful also passed safety and absorption screens, and motion tests supported their grip. Mounadi and colleagues present the shortlist as candidates for lab testing toward broad respiratory antivirals, not as ready medicines.
plos-pone-0356817: Etching silicon precisely is the foundation of the entire semiconductor industry. This paper studied the etching characteristics and profile simulation of silicon. The detailed etch science helps chipmakers carve ever-smaller features with confidence.
plos-pone-0357017:
Jung Ah Lim and colleagues argue that the standard yardstick for low muscle mass in older adults quietly measures fat as well. They propose a fix using Korean national survey data. Their 2026 study analyzed body scans from more than three thousand adults over sixty-five. It compared muscle indexed to height squared against a ratio. The ratio sets muscle in the arms and legs against muscle in the trunk.

The height-based index rose with body fat. Paradoxically, people it flagged as low-muscle had less metabolic syndrome. The trunk-relative ratio behaved oppositely. It fell as fat rose, flagged genuinely higher metabolic risk, and tracked insulin resistance even after fat was accounted for. The authors suggest the ratio gives doctors a cleaner read on muscle depletion in aging patients.
plos-pone-0355717:
Ruiheng Wu, Houmin Xing, and Jeffrey P Townsend re-analyzed whole genomes from 494 Chinese liver tumors, asking not just which mutations recur but which ones actually give cancer cells an edge. Their 2026 study computed, for every recurrent mutation, a scaled measure of the selective advantage it confers, using each gene's background mutation rate as the neutral yardstick.

The usual giants, including CTNNB1, TP53, and a famous regulatory hotspot, showed intense positive selection. More interestingly, several rare candidates, including genes tied to collagen chemistry and immune signaling, carried outsized effects, while some previously nominated drivers looked no better than neutral passengers. The authors stress the rare finds are computational priorities for laboratory proof, not established drivers.
plos-pone-0354817:
Kelly Holloway, Umair Majid, and Quinn Grundy interview Canadian doctors about prescribing immunoglobulin, a costly blood-plasma treatment whose demand keeps rising, in this 2026 qualitative study. Supply is limited worldwide, so doctors sit at the choke point between patients who need the treatment and a system trying to use it wisely. Twelve prescribing clinicians described how they actually make these decisions.

Three broad orientations emerged. Some doctors felt concern and uncertainty about prescribing at all. Others saw themselves as careful stewards of a scarce resource. A third group acted as advocates, pushing for their patients' access. The authors argue that policies built only on applying evidence mechanically miss these human stances, and that understanding them is essential for managing shortages fairly.
plos-pone-0354917:
Vladislav Soukhovolsky and colleagues modelled the flight and numbers of the conifer silk moth, a major forest pest across northern Eurasia. Foresters use light traps to track the moth, but catches are small when populations are low. Their 2026 paper draws on twenty-one years of trap records to build three linked models.

One model predicts when flight starts each season, using accumulated warmth after vegetation greens up in spring. That warmth total stayed stable year to year. A second model shows this year's catch depends mainly on the two previous years, matching known larval patterns. A third handles within-season catch shape. Together the models support forecasting pest numbers from trap data alone.
plos-pone-0353017:
Dane Wattle and co-authors documented the sea-floor life of key reefs in Australia's Groote Archipelago after back-to-back disasters. Mass coral bleaching and a tropical cyclone struck in quick succession, yet no formal benthic baseline existed for these waters. The archipelago's Traditional Owners, the Anindilyakwa people, hold deep sea knowledge but had not recorded reef change in survey form.

The 2026 study filmed reef sites and analysed frame composition to describe what covers the bottom now: coral, algae, rubble, and other benthic classes. Site health assessments accompany the inventory. Wattle and colleagues offer the baseline as shared ground for collaborative management, so future change can be measured against a documented starting point.
plos-pone-0355117:
Keji Shan and colleagues test in 2026 whether giving vitamin B12 together with a blue dye drug can ease septic shock in rats. Both agents alone have shown some promise when blood vessels lose tone badly. Rats were pretreated before a bacterial toxin triggered shock, and artery tissue was checked for gene changes alongside blood pressure, organ damage, and stress markers.

Combined treatment lowered several vessel relaxing signals, eased blood pressure problems in part, and reduced inflammation and tissue injury in lung, liver, and kidney. The authors link the benefit to a vessel wall pathway, while noting proof of cause still needs direct testing.
plos-pone-0355217:
Ivaan Pitua and six colleagues published this 2026 protocol, a detailed plan for a review of gout and high uric acid in people living with HIV. Modern HIV treatment has shifted attention toward long-term metabolic problems, and some widely used HIV drugs may raise uric acid. Nobody has yet totaled the worldwide burden.

Pitua's plan covers observational studies of adults, screened and scored by two reviewers working independently. The team will pool rates of high uric acid and gout, then compare results by drug era, region, and immune status. Registering the plan in advance keeps the later review honest and repeatable.
plos-pone-0353217:
Ali Aligholizadeh and three colleagues published this 2026 agriculture study of two friendly fungi that live inside plants. Isolated from native plants, the fungi Aspergillus micronesiensis and Penicillium momoi were pitted against three Fusarium strains that rot tomato and grain crops. The team also tested them under salty conditions and built a powder product.

One fungus fought by crowding the pathogens out, the other by chemical attack, and together they curbed growth strongly. Both tolerated salt, and their powder stayed viable for over two years. Aligholizadeh sees dual-purpose helpers for stressed fields.
plos-pone-0341617:
Christy Bills led a team of six authors on this 2026 community science study hunting flashing fireflies in the western United States. Western firefly populations were largely undocumented. Through outreach and a reporting website, volunteers across Utah sent in sightings over nearly a decade, and the team verified records with field visits and collected specimens.

More than a hundred and thirty new localities were documented, greatly widening the known range. Bills describes the hurdles, from stray reports to protecting private land, and plans expansion into neighboring states as a model for public-powered biodiversity research.
plos-pone-0354617:
Souleymane Abdou and Abdoul Moumouni Iro Sodo published this 2026 field study of quick-maturing cowpea in southeastern Niger. Cowpea feeds people and livestock across the Sahel, but drought, poor soils, weeds, and parasites cap yields. Twenty-one varieties were grown in six environments, and several stability methods judged which gave steady grain and fodder harvests wherever planted.

Environment shaped yields most, yet a set of named lines combined earliness with high, steady output of both grain and fodder. Abdou recommends wider testing across farming zones before release as climate-ready varieties for farmers.
plos-pone-0354717:
Saxton and colleagues, in a 2026 national survey study, estimate how a fairer blood donation rule would change who can give blood in New Zealand. Many countries long barred men from donating for a set period after sex with another man. New Zealand has moved to judging each donor's own behavior instead, and the team asked how many men that change would newly include.

More than three thousand men from this community answered an online survey. Most had donated before or wanted to, and most favored the individual approach. Under the old rule, only about one man in eight was eligible. Under the new individual assessment, that share rose to roughly four in ten. Newly eligible men tended to be in their thirties, more educated, and more connected to gay community life. The authors say the policy widens the donor pool safely.
plos-pone-0353417:
Da Zhang and seven colleagues read the map of Hebei Province in China through its place names, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. They catalogued more than eighteen hundred township names and tracked how names drawn from nature and from culture shifted over centuries. The study focuses on the transition belt where the Taihang Mountains meet the Great Wall corridor.

Nature-based names retreated toward the northeast mountains and coast, while culture-based names moved north. During the Ming and Qing dynasties the border belt shifted from military to civilian names. Slope, vegetation, migration, and ethnic mixing emerged as the main drivers — evidence that place names preserve a landscape's history long after events fade.
plos-pone-0353117:
Bewuketu Terefe, Nebiyu Mekonnen Derseh, and Tadesse Awoke Ayele map where young women across sub-Saharan Africa do and do not test for HIV, in this 2026 PLOS ONE spatial analysis. They pooled recent national survey data covering about one hundred and forty thousand women. Overall, fewer than four in ten had been tested — far short of global targets — and the map was strikingly uneven.

Testing clustered high in eastern and southern Africa and low in the west. Education, employment, media exposure, marriage, pregnancy, and wealth all nudged testing upward, while distance to a clinic dragged it down. The authors argue that blanket campaigns waste resources: the cold spots on the map need targeted outreach first.
plos-pone-0343917:
Sae-Lim and colleagues adapted a grief questionnaire for Thai caregivers in a 2026 study. The tool screens for grief that stays severe and long lasting after a loved one dies. Caregivers of patients with final-stage cancer often face that risk, but the original questions were written in English for other cultures.

The team translated the questions, had experts review them, and tested them with caregivers at a Bangkok hospital. Scores held steady over two weeks and lined up well with measures of worry, low mood, and caregiver strain. One weak question was dropped, leaving a short tool that Thai care teams can trust for screening.
plos-pone-0352317:
Sibel Balik and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One experiment on growing basil microgreens under LED lights in an indoor vertical farm. Light color recipes shape how these young greens grow and how nutritious they become. The team grew basil under three spectra: red-heavy mixes, a full spectrum, and one adding white and far-red light, then measured growth, color, and a long list of nutrients and flavor compounds.

The recipe with far-red produced the tallest plants, best yield, and brightest color, along with the most phenolic compounds. The full spectrum led on vitamin C, flavonoids, and oil content, while the red-blue mix gave the most dry matter and minerals. The authors recommend the far-red recipe for commercial growers, while noting results may differ by crop variety.
plos-pone-0352017:
Arta Grosmane-Bataraga and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study testing whether two blood proteins can serve as markers for myasthenia gravis, a disease in which the immune system weakens muscles. The proteins are useful in several brain and nerve diseases, so the team measured them in ninety patients and forty healthy volunteers, and compared levels with standard severity scores.

Neither protein differed between patients and controls, and neither tracked with disease severity, past crises, or treatments. The authors conclude plainly that these markers should not be adopted for monitoring this disease, despite their value elsewhere. As one of the larger controlled analyses of its kind, the study helps steer the search for myasthenia-specific blood markers in other directions.
plos-pone-0352417:
Vedran Premuzic and seven colleagues ask whether timing matters for a blood-filtering therapy in severe muscle injury. Their 2026 study covers intensive care patients in Croatia. Crushed or starved muscle releases toxins that can shut down the kidneys. Hemoadsorption scrubs some of those toxins from the blood. Thirty patients received it alongside standard dialysis-style support. Twenty-five comparable patients received the standard support alone.

Within the treated group, starting early made the difference. Patients whose filtering began within twelve hours of kidney injury recovered kidney function better. Blood levels of the muscle toxins myoglobin and creatine kinase were tracked for three days. Follow-up ran to sixty days. Because the study was small and retrospective, it cannot prove cause. Its title-stated association still gives intensive care teams a practical prompt: when this therapy is used, do not delay it.
plos-pone-0345817:
Md Minhajul, Md Rahman, and Md Tareque examine how moving house changes pregnancy care in Bangladesh. Their 2026 study uses the 2022 Demographic and Health Survey. Over forty-three hundred married women who had given birth in three years were analysed. Migration status sorted them into rural-to-urban movers, urban-to-rural movers, and stayers. The outcomes were receiving professional antenatal care and quality care, a stricter standard.

Rural-to-urban migrants did best of all. About sixty-nine percent received professional care, beating settled urban residents. Their adjusted odds were roughly half again higher. Urban-to-rural movers fared worst, falling below urban stayers. Quality care followed the same pattern, though levels were lower everywhere. Moving toward the city seems to carry women toward services, while moving away strands them. Maternal health programmes should track new arrivals in both directions, not just the cities swelling with newcomers.
plos-pone-0352117:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors have withdrawn a study that claimed a protein called ISL1 can push human stem cells to become heart muscle cells. Concerns were raised after the work came out. Several figures looked wrong in ways that are hard to explain as honest error.

In one chart, the error bars looked far too even across all time points. In gel images, sharp breaks showed between lanes. Bands in different rows also looked too much alike. The first author answered some points, but trust in the data was gone. Readers should not rely on the study's claims.
plos-pone-0350617:
Jingyi Dong and colleagues surveyed eleven hundred ten Chinese college students to learn how believing study matters turns into actually engaging with it. Values alone do not guarantee effort, so the team tested a chain: values may build confidence, confidence may feed motivation, and motivation may drive engagement. They separated self-driven motivation from pressure-driven motivation, since the two pull differently.

Confidence and both kinds of motivation each carried part of the effect from values to engagement, and the chain held in sequence. One wrinkle stood out: paths running through pressure-driven motivation weakened engagement instead of helping it. Students who study because they feel forced gain less from valuing education. For universities, the finding favors building confidence and genuine interest over piling on pressure.
plos-pone-0347517:
Ozgenur Cetinbag-Kuzu, Zehra Aydoğan, and Mustafa Gökcan adapted a music reward questionnaire into Turkish and proved the translation works. The questionnaire measures how much pleasure a person takes from music, split into facets. No checked Turkish version existed before. Two hundred sixty-six adults completed it, from non-musicians to professionals. A smaller group took it again three weeks later.

The Turkish form kept the original structure. Its scores were steady across the three-week gap, and its parts hung together well. The team also charted how scores vary with musicianship, gender, and age. Musical pleasure ranges from flat indifference to chills. It matters in brain and mental health research. Turkish researchers now hold a checked ruler instead of a rough translation.
plos-pone-0351117:
Heart rehabilitation programs coach patients toward lasting exercise habits, and Clare T M Doherty and colleagues asked participants what the coaching felt like from inside. Their 2026 PLOS One paper reports interviews and group talks nested inside a randomized trial for people with coronary heart disease.

Both coached and uncoached patients named surroundings and social support as key to staying active. The coached group described how sessions were delivered and which parts kept them engaged. Attendance records and personal diaries checked whether the program ran as planned. The findings are meant to help future programs keep patients moving after formal rehab ends.
plos-pone-0349617:
Inside cells, chemicals transform in webs of reactions, and knowing which way influence flows along each link is hard when only steady snapshots exist. Nava Leibovich and Miroslava Cuperlovic-Culf surveyed and tested methods for guessing that direction, in this 2026 PLOS One review of biochemical networks.

They benchmarked statistical scores and neural network approaches on artificial networks built to behave like real metabolism. A few methods succeeded when the underlying reaction rules were known; many others guessed poorly. The authors are candid about limits: direction in such webs may often be unrecoverable from still observations alone, a warning for anyone modeling cell chemistry from routine data.
plos-pone-0350117:
Old and leftover medicines pile up in homes, and most people bin them, sending chemicals toward soil and water. Maryam Farooqui and colleagues surveyed about eight hundred eighty adults in Qassim, Saudi Arabia, about what they keep and how they throw medicines away, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Seven in ten had unused medicines at home, often stored in the fridge. Nearly nine in ten tossed them in household trash, and almost none had ever been taught safe disposal. Most agreed pharmacies or authorities should offer take-back routes. The authors call for rules and collection programs to close the gap.
plos-pone-0351417:
Viruses being groomed as cancer killers and vaccine carriers must survive making, shipping, and storage. Sven Göbel and colleagues tested two such viruses, a Newcastle disease strain used against tumors and a chimeric yellow fever and Zika vaccine candidate, in this 2026 PLOS One stability study.

Both viruses shrugged off repeated freezing and thawing with little loss of infectious strength. Warmth was the enemy: above room temperature, infectious counts dropped substantially. Adding sugar as a stabilizer gave limited help. The authors map which steps of production and storage need cold control, practical knowledge for turning lab viruses into medicines that reach patients still potent.
plos-pone-0348117:
Cengizhan Kurt and colleagues asked whether a simple nutrition score can forecast death within a year after hip fracture surgery in older adults. Hip breaks kill up to four in ten older patients within a year, and poor nutrition worsens odds. Records covered more than six hundred patients aged sixty five and older at two large hospitals.

Just over one fifth of patients died within a year. Age, illness burden class, and the nutrition score each predicted death on their own when other factors were counted. The score sorted risk sharply: patients below a cut near ninety one died at vastly higher rates than those above it. A score from blood protein and body weight, the team argues, belongs in routine risk checks.
plos-pone-0351217:
Yongjia Deng and colleagues interviewed twenty patients in a university weight management clinic in West Virginia, a state with very high obesity rates. Guideline based clinics treat obesity as a medical condition, yet joining and staying takes trust. Talks covered why patients came, what helped, and what got in the way of care.

Patients prized kind, non judging staff and wanted more contact between visits. Support held firm even when policy shifts threatened coverage for their treatment, which patients noticed and valued. Personal inner drive brought many through the door. Cost and coverage gaps and social shame still burdened care. More touch points and steady respect, the study suggests, keep patients engaged.
plos-pone-0349417:
Marta Diaz-Guardamino and colleagues compare boat carvings on rocks in northwest Iberia and southern Scandinavia from late prehistory. High detail three dimensional records and map analysis were used on the Iberian carvings to read their forms and settings. Form by form comparison with Nordic boat art then tested how close the traditions really are.

Close matches in boat shapes support a late Bronze Age date for the Iberian carvings, roughly three thousand years ago. Nearly every Iberian site, even inland ones, kept a sight or travel link to navigable water. Shared boat art fits wide sea trade in metals like copper and tin across Atlantic Europe, mixed with ritual meaning for seafaring groups.
plos-pone-0350017:
Froucke van Gosliga and colleagues tested a pop up decision aid in hospital records to improve blood thinning shots that prevent clots in non surgical patients. Such shots are often missed despite clear guidance. Four hundred high risk patients were compared before and after the aid went live, with time trend methods used to strip out drift already under way.

Adequate prescribing rose from seventy eight to ninety one percent after launch. Once prior trend and timing patterns were counted, the clear gain shrank and could reflect chance. Baseline care was already strong at this site. Decision aids may still polish good practice, the authors conclude, but proof needs larger, multi site tests.
plos-pone-0350917:
Sicheng Huang and colleagues at public health departments in China set out in 2026 to design a shared information system for sudden health emergencies. Their case was Zhuhai, a coastal city, and the goal was a framework that could serve city, county, and local street or township offices alike.

Working from published research and expert discussion, the team drafted a set of measures, then asked a panel of experts to judge them through two rounds of voting. The finished city and county version has five main modules, while a simpler version serves the lowest level. Early use pointed to readiness and response as the parts that matter most, giving other Chinese cities a tested model to copy.
plos-pone-0350817:
Patrick Schmidt and Klaus G Nickel measured the stones used for tools at Sibhudu Cave in South Africa in 2026 work. Stone Age foragers there switched materials and tool shapes over a long span, and the team asked whether stone quality guided those choices.

Lab tests showed the local stones differ sharply: some flake easily but dull fast, others resist knapping yet stay strong in use. Stones needing less force were retouched more often, and long blades came mostly from stones that break predictably. Resistance to wear seemed to matter less. The pattern suggests skilled makers matched each stone to the job at hand.
plos-pone-0349317:
Zhe Zhu, Shan Huang, and Wanqiang Xu studied what makes Chinese charitable foundations good at raising money in 2026. Fundraising keeps such groups alive, and single cause answers rarely capture how nonprofit success is built.

Fifty-four foundations were compared with a method that looks for recipes of conditions rather than lone factors. Open digital reporting and active programs were near essential. Two winning recipes emerged, pairing those strengths with either political ties or strong professional management. The recipe view helps foundation leaders invest in bundles that work together, instead of chasing one fix at a time.
plos-pone-0348617:
Steve Joko, Christophe Antonio-Nkondjio, and co-authors combined a knowledge survey with blood testing in a village near Cameroon's capital to find out why malaria persists where awareness is high. Their 2026 study screened two hundred forty-nine residents for parasites and quizzed a subgroup in depth about what they know, believe, and actually do about the disease.

Knowledge and attitudes scored well and evenly across the village, yet daily practices lagged, though women practiced prevention better than men. A quarter of those screened carried malaria parasites, with school-age children hit hardest, evidence of quiet transmission without symptoms. Education showed mixed patterns depending on how groups were drawn. The authors call the core problem a knowledge-to-practice gap and urge interventions aimed at behavior and at the silently infected age group.
plos-pone-0349017:
Marco Antonio Morales-Osorio and colleagues present the plan for a clinical trial testing remote rehabilitation for fibromyalgia, a long-term condition marked by widespread pain and foggy thinking. The protocol describes a twelve-week program that pairs exercise guided by artificial intelligence with lessons that teach patients how pain works in the nervous system. Fifty adults will take part across several centers.

Half the patients will use an app that watches their movements and gives live feedback during three exercise sessions a week, plus a weekly pain lesson. The other half will receive enhanced usual care. Pain change is the main outcome the team will compare. No results are reported yet; the value lies in a careful test of care that could reach underserved regions.
plos-pone-0326717:
Liying Liu and colleagues wrote a step-by-step plan for giving drip drugs to mental health patients who act out with force. A drip is hard to start and hard to keep safe when a patient may pull the line or strike out, which puts both sides at risk. The team built the plan from past studies and talks with experts, and shaped it with a well-known quality model.

Experts then went through two rounds of review and reached firm, shared views on the draft. The final plan has three main parts, seventeen mid-level items, and forty-one fine points, from prep work to care after the drip ends. A shared plan like this gives ward staff one safe routine to follow in tense moments, not ad hoc choices.
plos-pone-0349117:
Yuri Kosaka and colleagues examined how high pressure inside the eye distorts cataract surgery planning. Surgeons calculate the artificial lens power from the eye's length, but pressure stretches the eye slightly, and when pressure drops the eye shrinks back, throwing off the calculation. The team reviewed nineteen eyes operated on for high pressure and compared measurements before and after.

Eye length and pressure moved together moderately, and each unit of pressure drop shortened the eye by a tiny, consistent amount. After surgery the average pressure fall was large and the eye shortened measurably. Predicted vision errors differed between the two standard formulas tested. Applying a length correction for pressure cases should sharpen the match between planned and actual vision after surgery.
plos-pone-0349217:
Chung-Yuan Huang and Sheng-Wen Wang simulated a familiar frustration: a game everyone agrees is excellent that almost nobody played. They combined two models of social behavior, one for how opinions spread and shift through conversation, and one for how people adopt a product once enough of their circle has. Virtual consumers were placed on four kinds of social network, from regular grids to hub-dominated webs.

Agents could talk themselves into or out of liking the product, then act on the result. The simulations show how praise can circulate widely while purchases stall, when thresholds for trying something new are never crossed in the right clusters. For marketers and designers, the model separates two problems that are usually confused: winning minds and triggering first tries are different battles.
plos-pone-0337817:
Cuc T T Nguyen and a large team tested whether a community programme could lift quality of life for rural Vietnamese adults whose blood pressure stays uncontrolled. Sixteen communities were assigned by chance to usual support or to an enhanced package adding personal storytelling sessions, home blood pressure monitoring, and expanded community health worker help. Just over six hundred and seventy patients were followed for a year with a standard health survey.

The enhanced group gained clearly on the physical side of quality of life at twelve months, by a margin the authors judge meaningful. Both groups received solid basic education about the condition. The authors present the package, built from neighbours' stories and home measurement rather than new drugs, as a workable model for rural chronic disease care in similar settings.
plos-pone-0348717:
Gilbert Mua Akwa and co-workers run the first injury surveillance of professional men's football in Cameroon, covering playoff tournaments in the top two leagues during one season. Africa has lacked such counts, though Europe tracks injuries closely. Their 2026 study has match-day medical officers log every injury needing attention across one hundred thirty-nine matches using standard forms.

One hundred seventy-one injuries were recorded, a high rate per hour of play. The second-tier league's rate ran more than double the top tier's. Legs took most knocks, cramps and bruises led the list, and a fifth of injuries were severe. Nearly half struck in the last half hour, pointing at fatigue. Better conditioning and medical readiness top the authors' advice.
plos-pone-0348017:
Xiaokun Zhang, Sunnan Li, and Chunzhou Zhao put eye-track specs on top women hoop stars. They asked how sweat level and shot spot change the eyes and the score. Twenty-two stars from a champ team shot from three spots. Each shot came at low, mid, or high work rates. The specs logged each glance at hoop, board, and net.

Mid work gave the lean gaze: few glances, short looks, best score. High work split the gaze and stretched the looks. More glances meant worse shots at all rates. Straight shots drew eyes to the hoop. Side shots drew eyes to the board. The team backs eye drills at game pace.
plos-pone-0346817:
Douwe van Hinsbergen and colleagues announce a big upgrade to a free web tool. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The tool, Paleolatitude.org, tells where a rock or fossil site sat on Earth long ago. That setting is key for reading ancient climates and life. The first version came out a decade ago.

Version three rests on a new global map of moving plates. It is the first such map to span the whole era of complex life. It also reports how unsure each answer is. Both the map's doubt and the sample's age feed that score. The shared tool lets climate and life scientists work from one moving Earth.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Cyprus's peacekeeping routine continued with Resolution 1517, adopted unanimously on 24 November 2003. The Secretary-General reported on 12 November about the UN operation. He urged both sides to address the fate of missing persons urgently. Cyprus's government agreed the UN force should stay past December. Conditions on the island left little choice.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 June 2004. They demanded an end to all remaining restrictions on the force. Violations at Strovilia drew sharp concern. Turkish Cypriot forces had altered positions there since June 2000. The Council insisted the earlier military balance be restored. A report on implementation was due by 1 June 2004.

The world court lost a senior judge in the summer of 1956. Judge Hsu Mo of China died on 28 June that year. His term on the bench still had years to run. Resolution 117, passed without a vote on 6 September 1956, set the way to fill his seat.

The Council chose the Assembly's next session for the vote. Judges there are picked by both big bodies at once. The eleventh session would host the ballot. Hsu Mo had served since the court's first days in 1946. He was a key figure in Chinese law. His death left one of the court's founding minds gone. The text is brief, a formal note of loss and a date for the cure.

Cambodia's peace settlement takes a step forward in Resolution 717, adopted in 1991. Draft agreements for a full settlement were ready, built on a framework the Council had backed in Resolution 668. The Supreme National Council of Cambodia had chosen Prince Norodom Sihanouk as its chairman, backed a voluntary ceasefire, and asked for UN staff to be sent quickly.

The Council approves the Secretary-General's plan and decides to set up a United Nations Advance Mission in Cambodia as soon as the settlement papers are signed. The mission's members are to head to Cambodia right after the signing. The Council calls on the Cambodian parties to work with the mission and welcomes the plan to reopen the Paris Conference so ministers can sign the agreements.

South Africa's crackdown on apartheid's opponents is condemned in Resolution 417, adopted on 31 October 1977. The Council noted reports of torture of political prisoners, deaths of detainees, and a wave of bans on people, groups, and news outlets since 19 October 1977. It recalled its 1976 condemnation of killings of African protesters, including schoolchildren in Soweto.

The Council strongly condemns the regime's mass violence and states its solidarity with those fighting apartheid. It demands an end to violence and repression. It demands freedom for everyone jailed under security laws or for opposing apartheid. It also demands a halt to killings in detention and torture. It also demands that bans on anti-apartheid groups and media be lifted. It demands that the Bantu education system end. It demands that majority rule based on justice and equality replace apartheid and the bantustan policy.

Weapons spilling out of Libya after its 2011 war are the worry in Resolution 2017, adopted on 31 October 2011. Arms of all kinds, above all shoulder-fired surface-to-air missiles, were spreading across the region. The Council feared they could fuel attacks by groups such as Al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb and unsettle the Sahel. Libya's chemical weapons stocks also still had to be destroyed.

The Council calls on Libya's authorities to stop the spread of arms, keep them in safe custody, and meet the country's arms control duties. It calls on Libya to keep working with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons to destroy its chemical stocks. States in the region are asked to weigh steps against this flow. The Libya sanctions committee, with its Panel of Experts, must judge the threats this spread poses and report with plans to counter it and guard stockpiles and borders.

War in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the setting for Resolution 1417, adopted on 14 June 2002. The UN Mission, MONUC, was still building toward its authorized strength. Killings and attacks in Kisangani in May had followed fighting there, and RCD-Goma held power in that city. The Inter-Congolese Dialogue at Sun City had made progress but produced no all-inclusive deal yet. Foreign forces were leaving, though slowly.

The Council extends MONUC until 30 June 2003 and calls on states to supply personnel up to the authorized 5,537. It holds RCD-Goma responsible for ending executions, rights abuses, and harassment in Kisangani and demands the city's demilitarization. It backs MONUC's work on disarming and sending home foreign fighters and its deployments to Kisangani and Kindu. It demands the total, speedy withdrawal of all foreign forces, with plans and timetables sent to MONUC. Reports are due at least every four months.

Afghanistan's UN mission is renewed behind the London Conference agenda in Resolution 1917, adopted on 22 March 2010. The London Conference of 28 January 2010 had set priorities under Afghan ownership. A Kabul conference was planned for later in the year. Taliban and Al-Qaida violence, civilian casualties, and the narcotics trade remained severe.

The Council extends the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, until 23 March 2011. UNAMA and the Special Representative continue to lead the international civilian effort. They co-chair the Joint Coordination and Monitoring Board to align donor support with Afghan priorities. They improve civil-military coordination with ISAF. They give good offices for Afghan-led reconciliation and reintegration within the sanctions framework. They support preparations for the 2010 national legislative elections. UNAMA must also help the government prepare the Kabul conference and the transition toward Afghan leadership on security, governance, and development.

Resolution 1617 is a Security Council decision adopted on 29 July 2005. It renewed and tightened sanctions against Al-Qaida, the Taliban, and people and groups tied to them. It builds on the sanctions system first set up in resolution 1267 in 1999. That system was restated in several later resolutions.

Under its terms, all states must freeze the funds of listed persons. They must also bar their travel and block arms sales to them. The text spells out what counts as being associated with Al-Qaida or the Taliban. It asks states to give a statement of case when proposing names for the Consolidated List. It also extends the Monitoring Team that helps the sanctions committee, for seventeen more months.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 17 was adopted in January 1946. It made three small changes to the Assembly's provisional rules of procedure. One change added words barring a committee from deciding political questions. One let a member with no seat on the General Committee attend and speak. That applied when its own agenda request was heard. One barred nominations under rule 73. A further change let the Economic and Social Council call world conferences on trade, prices, and health.

Resolution 69/17 is the General Assembly's programme-planning decision for the 2016–2017 period. It backs the findings of the Committee for Programme and Coordination on United Nations performance in 2012–2013 and on the proposed strategic framework. It fixes the organization's priorities for 2016–2017. They are economic growth and sustainable development, peace and security, and development of Africa. They are human rights, humanitarian coordination, and justice and international law. They are disarmament, and drug control and counter-terrorism. The Secretary-General is told to build the next programme budget around those aims.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Sierra Leone's peacekeeping mission gets only a few extra days in this brief text of 5 September 2000. UNAMSIL, the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, was backing a fragile peace process after years of civil war. In two short operative lines, the Council moved the mission's deadline to 20 September 2000. It also kept the country's situation under active review while it decided what should come next for the mission.

A question from its own fact-finding commission in Greece is answered on 10 February 1947. The Commission of Investigation, created weeks earlier, had asked whether it could request Greece to postpone executions of people sentenced to death for political offences. The question reached the Council while the commission was working in the region.

The commission, the Council ruled, had no power to ask Greece, Albania, Bulgaria, or Yugoslavia to delay any execution. There was one narrow exception. If the commission had reason to believe that hearing a condemned person as a witness would help its inquiry, it could ask for a postponement on that ground alone. The Secretary-General was to pass this reading of the mandate to the commission.

Rwanda tribunal short-term judges are allowed to finish the cases they have begun, in this text of 13 October 2006. Eighteen ad litem judges had been elected in 2003 for four years ending in June 2007. Several were mid-trial in cases that would not end before their terms expired, and the Secretary-General had asked the Council to act.

The ad litem judges named in the text may keep serving past their terms until the cases they are assigned to are completed. One judge may also be assigned to a further case as needed. States are asked again to make sure their nationals serving as ad litem judges are released to sit for the tribunal, so its completion strategy is not held up by staffing gaps.

The chemical precursors that turn Afghan opium into heroin are targeted on 11 June 2008. Afghanistan's drug trade fed terrorism, organized crime, and money laundering. The key chemicals, above all acetic anhydride, are legal in normal trade but are smuggled into Afghanistan for drug making.

All states are called on to tighten cooperation against drug production and trafficking in Afghanistan, including stronger tracking of the world trade in precursor chemicals. Exporting states are urged to notify importing countries of every shipment of the relevant chemicals when asked, under the 1988 drug convention. The aim is to stop legal shipments being diverted into heroin production while keeping lawful trade moving.

Southern Rhodesia's white minority rulers declared independence from Britain on their own in November 1965. Britain, the ruling power, treated the move as an act of rebellion. The Council adopted Resolution 217 on 20 November 1965 to answer the declaration.

The Council condemned the seizure of power by a racist settler minority. It said the declaration of independence had no legal validity. Britain was called on to crush the rebellion and end the minority regime at once. All states were told not to recognize the illegal authority. They had to cut off arms and military supplies. Economic ties had to be broken as well, including an embargo on oil and petroleum products.

Israeli forces had seized Syrian and Lebanese soldiers and security staff on Lebanese territory on 21 June 1972. An earlier resolution, passed that June, had already pressed for their release, without result. The Council returned to the matter in Resolution 317, adopted on 21 July 1972.

The Council reaffirmed the June resolution. It deplored the fact that the captured men had still not been freed. Work by the Council's president and by the Secretary-General had not secured their release. Israel was called on to return the men without delay. The president and the Secretary-General were also asked to make fresh efforts. Their task was to see the resolution carried out at last.

A new state from the former Yugoslavia sought a United Nations seat in 1993, but its name stood in the way. The applicant met the tests for membership set out in Article 4 of the Charter. A dispute had arisen over the state's name, and it had to be settled for the sake of calm in the region. Resolution 817 was adopted on 7 April 1993.

The Council recommended to the General Assembly that the state be admitted. Inside the United Nations, it would be referred to for the time being as "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia". That temporary name would hold for all United Nations purposes until the dispute was settled. The parties were urged to keep working with the co-chairmen of the peace conference on the former Yugoslavia. Their task was to reach a speedy settlement of the difference over the name.
un-sc-res-1517:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force gained six more months in November 2003. On 24 November 2003 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 June 2004. The government of Cyprus agreed the force should remain. The Secretary-General's report had called on the parties to address missing persons with urgency. That humanitarian issue ran alongside the military one. The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions, with 1251 of 1999 at their head.

Turkish Cypriot leaders and Turkish forces had to lift all limits on UNFICYP. The Council voiced concern at new breaches at Strovilia. It demanded the military position there as it stood before 30 June 2000. The force's freedom of movement was a standing sore point.
un-sc-res-117: Judge Hsu Mo of China died in June 1956, leaving a seat open at the International Court of Justice. On 6 September 1956 the Security Council set the election to fill the vacancy. The vote would take place during the General Assembly's eleventh session. The decision was taken without a formal vote. The text follows the standard wording of the court's statute. It does nothing beyond fixing the occasion for the election.
un-sc-res-717:
Cambodia's settlement gained a United Nations advance team in October 1991. The Paris framework of August 1990 had been endorsed by resolution 668 (1990). Draft accords for a full settlement were now on the table. Prince Norodom Sihanouk had been elected chairman of the Supreme National Council. The Cambodian parties had declared a voluntary ceasefire and renounced foreign military aid.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 30 September 1991. It decided to set up, under its authority, a United Nations Advance Mission in Cambodia, UNAMIC. The mission would deploy as soon as the Paris accords were signed. Its first tasks were to help the parties keep the ceasefire and to start mine awareness work. The Supreme National Council and the Cambodian parties were called to cooperate with the mission in full. The Council welcomed the plan to reconvene the Paris Conference at ministerial level.
un-sc-res-417:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 417 condemns South Africa's apartheid government for its violent crackdown on black citizens. The Council adopted the text on 31 October 1977. Reports told of torture of prisoners, deaths in detention, and bans on groups and newspapers.

The Council demands that the regime end its violence and free people jailed under security laws. It also demands an end to torture, to bans on the press, and to the Bantu education system. It asks governments to help victims, including students who fled the country. The Secretary-General had to report back by 17 February 1978.
un-sc-res-2017:
When the Council met on 31 October 2011, it adopted Resolution 2017 on Libya after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi, days after the civil war ended. Weapons from Libyan stockpiles were spreading across the region, and the Council feared they would reach armed groups.

The text calls on Libya's new leaders to secure all arms and guard them with care. It singles out shoulder-fired missiles that can bring down aircraft. It urges work with the global chemical weapons body to destroy Libya's chemical stocks. A sanctions panel must study the threat and propose ways to keep the weapons contained.
un-sc-res-1417:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1417 deals with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and its long war. The Council adopted it on 14 June 2002. Talks among Congolese parties at Sun City had raised hopes, but killings in Kisangani that May shocked the Council. Foreign troops still held parts of the country.

The text extends the United Nations mission, called MONUC, until 30 June 2003. States are asked to fill the mission up to its full strength of 5,537 troops. The Council condemns the Kisangani killings and holds the rebel group in charge there to blame. It demands the full and fast withdrawal of all foreign forces from the Congo.
un-sc-res-1917:
Resolution 1917 recorded the Council's decision on Afghanistan, adopted on 22 March 2010. The London Conference that January had set fresh goals under Afghan leadership. A Kabul conference was planned for later in the year. Taliban and Al-Qaida attacks still threatened civilians, aid workers, and Afghan forces.

The Council extends the assistance mission, called UNAMA, until 23 March 2011. The mission leads the civilian aid effort and backs Afghan ownership of the recovery. It will help prepare the 2010 parliamentary polls and support Afghan-led peace talks. The text ties security, honest government, and growth together. It also presses for stronger regional cooperation and better protection of civilians.
un-sc-res-1617:
Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1617, adopted on 29 July 2005. The threat had shifted since the first sanctions text in 1999. Groups used the internet for propaganda and recruitment. The Council wanted a clear test for who counts as linked to the networks.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo on listed names. It defines being associated with the networks to cover funding, planning, arming, and recruiting for them. States must file a written case when they propose a name. Lost passports must be voided fast and shared through Interpol. The expert Monitoring Team is extended for seventeen months.
europmc-pmc10017517:
Zecchini and a large team report that a cell chemical called fumarate can trigger the release of mitochondrial DNA and switch on immune defenses, in a 2023 study. Mutations that block the breakdown of fumarate cause a rare inherited condition with kidney cancer. Fumarate then builds up inside cells to high levels.

The team traced how that buildup pushes DNA out of the cell's powerhouses in tiny packages. The loose DNA acts as an alarm signal to the immune system. The finding links cell fuel use to immune activity in a new way.
europmc-pmc10034917:
Sharma and co-authors review current and emerging ideas about the tumor microenvironment in glioblastoma, in a 2023 paper. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive common brain tumor in adults. Its surroundings mix cancer cells with brain cells, immune cells, and blood vessels in a dense, shifting web.

The review describes how that web feeds the tumor and shields it from drugs and immune attack. It surveys new treatment ideas that target the surroundings rather than the tumor alone. Readers get a clear picture of why this cancer resists care and where hope lies.
europmc-pmc10465717:
The GBD 2021 Anaemia Collaborators charted anaemia across the world from 1990 to 2021. Anaemia means the blood carries too little haemoglobin, the part that moves oxygen. The study spans 204 nations and areas, split by age and sex. It also weighs 37 root causes of the condition.

In 2021, 24.3% of all people had anaemia, a total of 1.92 billion cases. That share had fallen from 28.2% in 1990, yet case counts rose with population growth. Young children, women, and people in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia bore the worst load. The condition cost 52.0 million years of healthy life that year. Lack of iron in food was the top cause.
europmc-pmc10544417:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed cancer-linked fibroblasts in 2023 and fresh ways to use them in immune therapy. Fibroblasts build the support web around a tumour. They can speed blood vessel growth, spread, and drug resistance. They also reshape the zone to shield the tumour from immune attack.

Yet the group is far from uniform, Zhang stresses. Some subtypes slow tumour growth rather than aid it. That split means drugs must strike with care, aimed at the harmful kinds alone. The review sums up where these cells arise and how subtypes differ. It tracks trials that target them across many cancers. Early immune therapy pairs that include them get a close look.
europmc-pmc10904817:
Qian and colleagues review a family of helper proteins that run cell energy systems in this 2024 paper. The PGC-1 family has three members that switch on genes for mitochondria, the parts of cells that make energy. They also help control cell stress, swelling, and the folding of new proteins. Faults in them are tied to many diseases.

The review maps what turns these helpers up or down and which partners they work with. It then traces their roles in cancers, heart disease, brain disorders, kidney disease, and metabolic ills, meaning diseases of how the body handles fuel. The review weighs their value as markers for diagnosis and for judging a patient's outlook. It also surveys early lab studies of therapies that target these proteins.
europmc-pmc11059217:
Kim and colleagues review natural cell sacs as delivery vehicles for therapy in this 2024 paper. Exosomes are nano-sized sacs cells secrete, and they carry proteins, fats, and nucleic acids between cells. They mix well with body tissue, load varied cargo, and reach deep into tissue. Those traits make them attractive as drug carriers.

The review covers their use in chemotherapy, gene therapy, and heat-based cancer therapy. Because sacs from a patient's own cells are recognised as self, they open a path to personalised treatment. Three hurdles are named plainly: weak cargo loading, fragile structure, and unclear origins of mixed sac batches. The authors call for large-scale production with tight quality control and for more animal and human trials. They still rate sacs as efficient, stable, and safe carriers in prospect.
europmc-pmc11149917:
Jiang and a large team evaluate a broad RAS-blocking drug in lab models and patients in this 2024 study. RAS proteins act as growth switches, and faulty versions drive many cancers. Earlier drugs blocked only one faulty form. Their compound, RMC-6236, targets the active, GTP-loaded state of RAS across many forms. GTP is the small molecule that switches RAS on.

Broad blockade with RMC-6236 was active at doses that were tolerated, the team reports. At those doses it drove profound tumour regressions in animal and cell models of cancers driven by RAS. The same exposures were associated with objective responses in patients, meaning measurable tumour shrinkage. The paper presents both the lab evaluation and the early patient evidence. It frames the drug as a candidate for the wide set of cancers that RAS mutations drive.
europmc-pmc11165417:
Zhang and colleagues pool global data on excess weight in children and teens in this 2024 systematic review. Overweight and obesity in youth raise the risk of lifelong disease. Rates vary by country and have climbed in many places. The team set out to measure the global prevalence and to sort the risk factors behind it.

Across the pooled studies, overweight and obesity proved highly prevalent in children and adolescents, the authors found. Risk factors fell into three groups: inherent factors, dietary factors, and environmental factors. Inherent covers traits a child is born with, while the other two cover food and surroundings. The authors conclude that excess weight is common in this age group worldwide. They call for control measures that act on behaviour, environment, and culture together, not on diet alone.
europmc-pmc1180517:
Holmes and colleagues reported a 2005 genome study of human influenza A virus. They compared 156 complete genomes of the H3N2 type. All samples came from New York State between 1999 and 2004. Tracking how flu changes helps experts pick vaccine strains each year.

Several virus lines were found living side by side in the same seasons. Gene segments had swapped between lines in repeated mixing events. One swap gave later viruses a key surface gene. Holmes links that swap to the Fujian-like outbreak of 2003 to 2004. The work appeared in PLoS Biology.
europmc-pmc1187917:
Brach and colleagues studied walking width and falls in 2005. Older adults often fall, and unsteady gait raises that risk. Speed and stride timing had known links to falls. Step width shifts, how much side-to-side spacing varies, were less clear.

Gait was recorded for 503 adults with an average age of 79. All could walk on their own in daily life. Both very steady and very uneven step widths tied to fall history. The link held for people walking at near normal speed. Brach suggests width balance, not just steadiness, signals fall risk.
europmc-pmc1236917:
Kahn proposed a new body measure for heart risk in 2005. Body mass index, or BMI, may not capture fat risk well. His lipid accumulation product uses waist size and blood fat level. Both values reflect excess fat stored around organs.

Data came from a national survey of about 9,180 adults. The new measure was compared with BMI across 11 risk factors. Many adults ranked high on one measure but not the other. Kahn found the lipid product flagged risk better overall. A tape measure plus a blood test may beat height and weight alone.
europmc-pmc1241417:
Birnbaum and Fenton reviewed cancer risk from early-life chemical exposure in 2003. Developing bodies grow and change fast, which raises their sensitivity. Human data link prenatal radiation clearly to later cancer. Parental chemical exposure hints at brain tumors and leukemia in children.

Animal studies show early exposure to many chemicals raises tumor rates. Prenatal estrogens, natural and synthetic, raise breast and vaginal tumors in people. Halogenated chemicals raise liver tumors after early exposure. Dioxin also delays breast tissue development in rodents. Birnbaum argues hormone disruptors deserve cancer scrutiny from the earliest ages. The pair wrote for Environmental Health Perspectives. Young mice and rats were the test stock in most of this work. Birth and the first days of life are the key time frame here.
europmc-pmc1314917:
Lewis and the Kenya Aflatoxicosis Investigation Group surveyed market maize during a deadly outbreak in 2005. In April 2004, aflatoxin poisoning struck rural Kenya. It caused 317 cases and 125 deaths. Homegrown maize was the known source, but market maize was unchecked.

Surveys covered 65 markets and 243 vendors in affected districts. Of 350 products tested, 55 percent topped the Kenyan limit of 20 parts per billion. Seven percent exceeded 1,000 parts per billion. The worst district averaged 52.91 versus 7.52 in the least affected. Lewis ties market contamination to outbreak geography. 35 percent of products also topped 100 parts per billion. Local farm maize most often crossed the limit.
europmc-pmc1468417:
Tuberculosis germs carry a DNA stretch that varies by strain, letting labs type them fast. Brudey and co-authors mined the fourth world database of those types in 2006. The method, spoligotyping, reads the pattern of gaps in that stretch. The database held 39,295 strains from 122 countries.

The team sorted them into 1,939 shared types and 62 broad lineages. The update added 26 new families tied to place. A blind computer check backed most of the groupings. Brudey shows the resource maps how TB strains spread and relate across the globe. It aids labs, outbreak work, and studies of the germ's past.
europmc-pmc1501017:
Programmed cell death may help destroy lung tissue in COPD. Demedts and co-authors reviewed that idea in 2006. COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, involves airway swelling and loss of lung tissue, mostly from cigarette smoke. Apoptosis is the body's tidy way of killing off cells.

Lungs of COPD patients hold more dying wall and vessel cells than healthy lungs. New cell growth does not keep pace, so tissue thins into emphysema. Animal work points to a growth factor, VEGF, whose loss triggers such death. Demedts suggests blockers of death enzymes, like caspase-3, could one day slow the loss of lung tissue.
europmc-pmc2040517: Oxytocin increases generosity in humans. — a 2005 science paper on oxytocin and generosity. It finds oxytocin boosts giving for labs worldwide. The paper is the generosity study: the findings on oxytocin for labs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2214817: A novel CpG island set identifies tissue-specific methylation at developmental gene loci. — a 2005 science paper on a CpG island set. It identifies the tissue methylation. The paper is the island-set study: the findings on methylation, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2253517: LTRharvest, an efficient and flexible software for de novo detection of LTR retrotransposons. — a 2005 science paper on the LTRharvest tool. It detects the LTR retrotransposons. The paper is the LTRharvest guide: the findings on the software tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2267817: Dynamic remodeling of individual nucleosomes across a eukaryotic genome in response to transcriptional perturbation. — a 2005 science paper on DNA-spool reshuffling. It charts the spool reshuffling for labs. The paper is the spool study: the notes on DNA ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2447617: Improved outcomes from the administration of progesterone for patients with acute severe trauma — a 2008 science paper on progesterone for brain trauma. It improves the trauma outcomes. The paper is the outcome study: the findings on trauma ills, filed here in session.
