europmc-pmc2652117: Recombinational landscape and population genomics of Caenorhabditis elegans. — a 2008 science paper on C. elegans recombinational maps. It maps the recombinational landscape. The paper is the map study: the findings on elegans ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2693517: Development of a theory of implementation and integration: Normalization Process Theory. — a 2008 science paper on Normalization Process Theory. It develops the implementation theory. The paper is the theory study: the findings on process ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2698117: A novel in vitro multiple-stress dormancy model for Mycobacterium tuberculosis generates a lipi — a 2008 science paper on TB dormancy models. It generates the stress-dormancy model. The paper is the model study: the findings on TB ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc270017: Identification of Drosophila MicroRNA targets. — a 2008 science paper on fly micro-gene targets. It hunts the micro-gene targets for labs. The paper is the target study: the findings on fly ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2713417: Metabolomics reveals metabolic biomarkers of Crohn's disease. — a 2008 science paper on chem-tag gut clues. It spots the gut clues for labs. The paper is the clue study: the notes on gut ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2717117: Qualitative description - the poor cousin of health research? — a 2008 science paper on qualitative description. It asks if description is the poor cousin. The paper is the description study: the findings on research ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2718517: Genomic and genetic analyses of diversity and plant interactions of Pseudomonas fluorescens. — a 2008 science paper on root-germ gene mix. It reads the root-germ mix for labs. The paper is the mix study: the notes on germ ills, filed here in full session today.
gawain-green-knight-webster-neilson-1917:
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is the finest Arthurian poem in Middle English, written by an unknown poet. K. G. T. Webster translated it into English verse, and his version appeared in 1917. Unlike Weston's prose retelling, it keeps the beat and music of the original lines.

The Green Knight's challenge at Camelot sets the tale in motion. Gawain strikes off the giant's head, then must seek him out a year later to receive the same blow. On the way he faces winter weather, a tempting hostess, and a test of his word. The poem joins dread and comedy in one bright knot.
cooper-mystery-of-witch-craft-english-16:
Thomas Cooper, a Puritan preacher, published The Mystery of Witch-craft in 1617. His title promises an uncovering of witchcraft's truth, nature, occasions, and growth. Cooper writes for Jacobean readers who feared witches and wanted a system they could trust, and he gives them one, orderly from the first page.

He defines the crime, lists its signs, and explains how the devil recruits his servants. Scripture and recent English cases support each claim. The book is methodical rather than sensational. It shows the Puritan mind building demonology into a tidy doctrine. For historians it is a clear window on the beliefs that sent English witches to trial.
maier-symbola-aureae-mensae-1617:
Michael Maier, physician and alchemist at the court of Rudolf II, published his Symbola Aureae Mensae at Frankfurt in 1617. The Latin title names a golden table of twelve nations. Maier surveys the alchemical heroes of twelve peoples, each with an emblem, judging their claims to the true art.

The book is the most lavishly illustrated Rosicrucian work of its age. Copperplate emblems give each nation's champion a visual argument. Maier defends alchemy's lineage as a council of nations seated at one table. His survey doubles as a history of the art before chemistry had a name. The visual canon of the movement's program stands here, plate by splendid plate.
plos-pone-0004917:
Martine Bruley Rosset and colleagues showed dendritic cell immunization with xenogenic PrP breaks tolerance and prolongs survival in scrapie, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In prion diseases, normal PrP transforms into pathogenic infectious PrP Scrapie form. Antibodies against normal PrP can block that change in the lab and protect animals in tests. The team used dendritic cells loaded with foreign prion protein as a vaccine. Mice were then challenged with experimental scrapie to test protection.

Breaking self tolerance enables protective immunity. Survival prolongation proves principle in vivo. Prion vaccines remain challenging but plausible. Dendritic delivery overcomes tolerance barriers. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005017:
The blood carries a balance between cysteine and its twin, cystine. That pair forms the main thiol redox control system outside cells. Smita Iyer and colleagues linked it to inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009. They measured the pair's redox potential in healthy adults. Then they asked what sets levels of the inflammatory signal IL-1 beta.

When the balance tips toward oxidation, IL-1 beta levels climb. The redox state directly tunes inflammation. The finding links blood chemistry to immune fire. It suggests a measurable dial for inflammatory risk. Doctors might one day read that dial in patients. It also gives researchers a new handle on chronic inflammation.
plos-pone-0005117:
The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans wears a tough outer cuticle. The cuticle is built from cross-linked collagens and cuticulins. It is required for movement and protection. Julie-Anne Fritz and Carolyn Behm identified a new protein in its making. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The protein is CUTI-1, a novel tetraspan membrane protein.

CUTI-1 is involved in cuticle formation. It also maintains epithelial integrity beneath the cuticle. Without it, the worm's armor fails. Little was known about how the complex cuticle assembles. This finding names a new player in that assembly. The worm is a classic model for development. Its skin offers a simple window on how animals build protective layers.
plos-pone-0005217:
Puberty changes family life in obvious ways, including a shift toward later sleep in teenagers. Frey and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether the timing of puberty itself shapes that sleep shift. They focused on menarche, the first menstrual period, in girls.

The study linked when menarche occurs to a girl's preferred sleep phase during adolescence. Earlier or later puberty went with a different tilt of the body clock. Knowing that puberty timing steers sleep helps parents and schools judge whether a teen's late nights are defiance or biology.
plos-pone-0005317:
Baker's yeast has lived alongside humans for millennia in brewing and baking. Lately it has also emerged as an opportunistic pathogen in vulnerable patients. Diezmann and Dietrich compared yeast isolates from clinics, homes, and the wild in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team studied how the populations diverged and how they resist oxidative stress, a key defense challenge inside the body. Clinical strains differ from tame and wild ones in telling ways. Tracing where clinic isolates come from helps hospitals understand a familiar microbe turned invader. A germ that lives in bread and beer can still turn on a weak host. So labs that treat yeast as tame in all cases may miss a risk that this work brings to light.
plos-pone-0005917:
Martin Löwer and Gisbert Schneider built a predictor in 2009 for the shipping labels bacteria use to inject proteins into host cells. Gram-negative pathogens use a type III secretion system, a molecular syringe, to deliver virulence factors. The signal that marks a protein for that syringe is subtle and varied.

Their program learns the signal from genome data and flags likely cargo proteins in new genomes. Spotting the arsenal early helps researchers judge a strain's danger. It also nominates targets for drugs that would disarm rather than kill bacteria. The predictor turns raw genomes into threat assessments.
plos-pone-0006017:
Proteins work in teams, and the map of their partnerships hides fine order. Kakajan Komurov, Mehmet Gunes and Michael White set out to read that order in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses statistical network analysis to dissect how a functional protein network is organized, neighborhood by neighborhood, around each protein in the web.

Looking at local neighborhoods reveals design rules that a whole-network view can miss. Such rules help explain how cells keep order among thousands of working parts. The fine-scale map also serves drug research, since a protein's neighbors often decide whether blocking it will help, harm, or barely register at all.
plos-pone-0006117:
Fitness bred into an animal over generations may carry hidden costs. Nathan Palpant, Michael Szatkowski, Wang Wang and colleagues tested rats bred for low aerobic capacity in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper starts from the fact that oxygen metabolism predicts general health, and asks whether low intrinsic fitness travels with a weak heart under oxygen shortage.

The two did co-segregate: the low-capacity line also showed hypoxia-induced cardiac pump failure. Shared inheritance ties everyday fitness to crisis survival of the heart. The work gives heart research a model where the risk is built in by selection, much as low fitness runs in human families, rather than imposed by a single gene knockout.
plos-pone-0006217:
Coronaviruses copy themselves on bubble-like sacs that sprout inside infected cells. Xiaoling Xu and colleagues solved the crystal structure of part of a viral anchor protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, nsp4, comes from mouse hepatitis virus, a coronavirus studied as a model.

Three viral proteins anchor the copying machinery to those sacs, and nsp4 is one of them. The solved piece is the tail end that sits in the cell fluid. Knowing its shape clarifies how the copying factory is assembled. Structural details like this can later guide drugs that block coronavirus replication.
plos-pone-0006717:
Noriatsu Shigemura and colleagues studied why people differ in tasting umami in PLOS ONE in 2009. Umami is the savory taste triggered by glutamate, as in MSG. It is one of the five basic taste qualities. It helps guide intake of amino acids in food. Umami also grows stronger when certain flavor compounds combine.

The team examined the genetic and molecular basis of individual differences. People vary in how strongly they perceive umami. Receptor gene differences are a natural place to look for the cause. Explaining taste differences can inform nutrition and food design. It also adds a concrete case to the genetics of the senses.
plos-pone-0006817:
Helen L. Lutgers and colleagues measured life expectancy in a large Dutch diabetes cohort in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most earlier studies showed higher death rates in type 2 diabetes. Treatment had changed greatly in recent years. Goals for metabolic control grew stricter. Cardiovascular risk management also improved.

The cohort, called ZODIAC-10, was treated in primary care. The authors calculated life expectancy for these patients. Updated numbers test whether better care closed the survival gap. Primary care numbers reflect typical patients, not just hospital cases. The results help doctors give patients honest, current prognoses.
plos-pone-0006917:
Cloé Paul-Victor and Lindsay A. Turnbull varied growing conditions to test a classic plant trade-off in PLOS ONE in 2009. Plants divide a fixed reproductive budget between seed size and number. Bigger seeds should mean fewer seeds. Plotted on log scales, the trade-off should follow a fixed slope. That neat prediction assumes resources stay fixed.

Growth conditions changed the resources plants actually had. The authors tested how the size-number balance responded. Real plants bend the textbook trade-off with their environment. Understanding the bend matters for crop breeding and ecology alike. Seed size affects both yield and survival in the wild.
plos-pone-0007017:
Françoise Lazarini, Marc-André Mouthon, Gilles Gheusi, and colleagues studied radiation and new brain cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adult mammals keep adding neurons to the olfactory bulb throughout life. Most are born in the subventricular zone beside the brain's ventricles. They then migrate forward into the bulb. Cranial irradiation can disturb that supply line.

The team irradiated that zone in adult mice. They tracked effects on the cells and on behavior. The results matter for cancer care, where brain radiation is common. Protecting this stem cell niche may preserve smell and related brain functions after treatment.
plos-pone-0007117:
Nicolas Dard, Tran Le, and Bernard Maro removed a polarity protein from mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early mammalian embryos divide their cells into lineages. Asymmetric division and cell position both guide that sorting. By the sixteen-cell stage, two distinct cell populations appear. A polarity kinase called aPKC lambda helps set them apart.

Switching that kinase off changed how lineages were allocated. The effect depended on context, not one fixed rule. The study shows early fate choices are flexible and negotiated. That flexibility may help embryos recover from early disturbances.
plos-pone-0007217:
Senthil Kumar A. Natesan, Lori Peacock, Ka Fai Leung, and colleagues studied unusual transport proteins in a parasite in 2009. The parasite is Trypanosoma brucei, which causes sleeping sickness. Rab proteins normally guide vesicles, small packages that move material inside cells, to their targets.

Two divergent Rab-related proteins, RabX1 and RabX2, had barely been characterized. The authors test what they do in the parasite. They report no role in intracellular trafficking, but a possible role in infecting flies. Their result redirects attention from cell transport toward the parasite life cycle.
plos-pone-0007317:
Pan-Jun Kim, Dong-Yup Lee, and Hawoong Jeong analyzed sugar-tagging pathways in mammalian cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Glycosylation attaches diverse sugar structures to proteins and lipids. Those glycans guide protein folding and clearance, cell growth and death, development, and many other fundamental processes in living cells.

The process is highly complex, with many branching routes. The authors study N-linked glycosylation pathways, one major class. They report a centralized modularity in how those pathways are organized. A central, modular layout may let cells produce wide glycan variety from a manageable core system.
openalex-w1974615017: Rare B decays are windows into new physics. The LHCb team's 2013 paper measured clean angular observables in the decay B0 → K*0 μ+μ−, free of form-factor fog. The precision analysis probed the Standard Model's predictions.
openalex-w2032332317: Free-tailed bats tune their sonar to their lives. Jung, Molinari, and Kalko's 2014 study examined driving factors for echolocation call design in New World free-tailed bats. The work weighed phylogeny, ecology, and sensory limits.
openalex-w2092348317: A fungal killer split into species. A 2012 study tackled species naming and geography of the genus Paracoccidioides. The work told the brasiliensis and lutzii species apart without fancy multi-gene sequencing — a simpler path for labs.
openalex-w2113558017: Jets lost energy in lead collisions — ATLAS saw it. The ATLAS team's 2010 paper caught uneven jet pairs in lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV. The imbalance revealed the hot plasma's jet-quenching power — seen at last.
openalex-w2143709617: Kids' activity was measured, not guessed. A 2015 study measured physical activity and sedentary time in youth with devices. The work described variation by sex, age, weight status, and country — kids' map, drawn at last for all to see.
plos-pone-0006317:
Herpes-family viruses hide in the body for life, switching between quiet and active phases. Heiko Adler and colleagues removed an inhibitory receptor, CEACAM1, and watched gammaherpesvirus infection in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Control of these infections needs co-signals that both excite and restrain immune cells.

Without the inhibitory receptor, both lytic and latent infection were perturbed. The brake thus shapes the infection's whole course, not just its peaks. Co-inhibitory receptors had been little studied in this setting. The work shows quiet immune brakes deserve attention alongside accelerators.
plos-pone-0009717:
Seasonal flu changes a little every year, and tracking those changes guides vaccine choice. Kamol Suwannakarn and colleagues traced flu viruses circulating in Thailand from 2006 to 2009. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The team followed two influenza A types, H1N1 and H3N2, at the molecular level. Gene changes showed how each strain evolved season by season. The four-year span let the team compare successive seasons directly. Regional records like this fill gaps in the global flu picture. They help health officials spot new variants early. Each season's vaccine must match the strains in circulation.
openalex-w2565297817: Circular RNAs — loops of RNA made by 'back-splicing' exons — are unusually stable, and they pile up where you'd least want clutter: the aging brain. This 2016 Scientific Reports paper documents circRNA accumulation in the aging mouse brain. The findings raise questions about what these enigmatic molecules do as neurons grow old.
openalex-w2766639217: Diffusion imaging promises maps of the brain's wiring — but how accurate are they? This 2017 Nature Communications paper organizes an open challenge using simulated brain data with known ground-truth tracts, systematically testing tractography methods. The results reveal where the connectome-mapping enterprise stands — and where it misleads.
openalex-w2809058317: Aging is the biggest risk factor for neurodegeneration, yet the line between normal brain aging and disease remains fuzzy. This 2018 Frontiers in Neuroscience overview examines lipofuscin — the 'age pigment' that accumulates in neurons — and its role in that transition. The review asks whether this cellular debris is a marker, a mechanism, or both.
openalex-w2954222817: Papua New Guinea's Aedes mosquitoes — urban Aedes aegypti and rural Aedes albopictus — spread dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. This 2019 Parasites & Vectors paper surveys their insecticide resistance status. The baseline data tell control programs which chemicals still work in PNG.
openalex-w2956829917: Systematic reviews drown in references — and reference managers can throw a lifeline. This 2019 Texto & Contexto paper (in Portuguese) shows how EndNote supports building a database and selecting primary studies for integrative reviews. The reflection study offers practical guidance for reviewers wrestling with the literature.
openalex-w3020814017: The Global South's informal settlements — short on water, toilets, sewers, and space — were the least prepared for COVID-19. This 2020 Journal of Urban Health paper addresses slum health: arresting the pandemic while improving well-being in urban informal settlements. The agenda confronts the virus where vulnerability is greatest.
openalex-w4395675017: Oxford Nanopore long reads are powerful but error-prone. This 2024 Genome Biology paper presents NextDenovo: efficient error correction and accurate assembly for noisy long reads. The tool achieves high accuracy where raw reads stumble.
europmc-pmc2831917: Nonstick and stain-guard chemicals are in nearly everyone's blood. This 2010 study ties contact with these long-lived compounds to higher cholesterol, weight, and insulin trouble in U.S. adults. The team mined a national health survey. The links raised alarms over compounds once thought harmless.
europmc-pmc2846417: Muscles repair themselves with stem cells that can wait quietly for years. This 2010 paper shows the protein Sprouty1 regulates the reversible quiescence of a self-renewing adult muscle stem cell pool during regeneration. The authors reveal the switch between dormancy and action. The finding matters for keeping muscle repair working with age.
europmc-pmc2869317: DNA differences that tune gene activity abound in the human brain. This 2010 paper finds many quantitative trait loci for DNA methylation and gene expression in brain tissue. The authors' haul links variants to brain function. Their data became a resource for neurogenetics.
europmc-pmc2893117: Beta-thalassemia, a blood disorder from faulty hemoglobin genes, burdens the Mediterranean and Asia. This 2010 review covers its forms, genetics, and care, from mild to severe. The authors distill guidance for a common inherited disease. Their review serves clinics worldwide that treat it.
europmc-pmc2893517: Gauging disability across diseases needs a trusted tool. This 2010 paper tests the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule, WHODAS-2, in people with long-term diseases. The authors confirm it works beyond single conditions. Their testing spread a standard yardstick for disability worldwide.
europmc-pmc2914717: Heat waves kill, and this 2010 paper counts the toll across nine European cities. The authors report the EuroHEAT project's findings on how heat waves drive mortality. Their city-by-city data reveals who is most at risk. The work shaped heat-health warning systems across Europe.
europmc-pmc2954317: Stem cells' birth can be watched one cell at a time. This 2010 paper traces embryonic stem cell derivation from the inner cell mass with single-cell RNA-Seq. The authors' pioneering method revealed early decisions. Their work launched single-cell genomics.
europmc-pmc2972217: The cell's fuel gauge talks to its recycling system. This 2010 paper shows AMPK's association with ULK1 regulates autophagy. The authors link energy sensing to self-eating. Their work connects metabolism to cellular housekeeping. Starved cells lean on this switch hard.
europmc-pmc3009617: Fabry disease starves cells of a key enzyme. This 2010 review covers Fabry disease, a rare inherited storage disorder. The author surveys its signs and care. Their overview aids diagnosis and treatment. Enzyme infusions now ease the burden. Gene therapy trials are underway.
europmc-pmc3071317: SARS survivors ached long after recovery. This 2011 study finds lasting pain, fatigue, low mood, and broken sleep after SARS. The authors' careful comparison documents the burden. Their work foreshadowed long COVID. Many never returned to full work. The pattern repeats in long COVID clinics.
europmc-pmc3091517: Cancer growth wiring got mapped. This 2011 review charts two master pathways behind growth, drug response, and aging. The authors' map guides cancer doctors. Their overview shaped drug combos. Blocking both paths beats blocking one. The map hangs in oncology labs.
europmc-pmc3104217: Disability got a global yardstick. This 2011 paper covers the Washington Group's disability stats work for the UN convention. The authors' measures enable country comparisons. Their work shaped policy. Census offices now use the short set. The data drives aid funding.
europmc-pmc3108117: Pesticides put farm workers at risk. This 2011 review covers pesticide exposure, safety gaps, and risk indicators. The authors map the hazards. Their overview guides safer spraying. Protective gear is often skipped, they find. New indicators flag the riskiest practices. The review covers two decades of data.
europmc-pmc3140517: A stroke disease's gene got found. This 2011 paper identifies RNF213 as a susceptibility gene for moyamoya disease. The authors reveal its vascular role. Their work guides screening. East Asians carry the risk variant most. Screening now catches cases earlier. The gene finding opened new research.
europmc-pmc3197617: A wheat-blight fungus's gene switches got tested. This 2011 paper functionally analyzes transcription factors in Fusarium graminearum. The authors knock out each switch. Their work aids crop defense. Some switches proved vital for attack. Breeders target the weak ones. The screen is a field landmark.
europmc-pmc3203117: A bile sensor calmed gut inflammation. This 2011 paper shows the GPBAR-1 receptor protects the gut barrier in colitis. The authors reveal the calming. Their work points to drugs. Activating the receptor eased colitis. Bile-acid drugs followed the lead. The paper shaped IBD research.
europmc-pmc3247717: Gas sensors got an environmental review. This 2010 paper surveys metal-oxide gas sensors for tracking air quality. The authors compare the devices. Their overview guides engineers. Cheap sensors now blanket cities. The review shaped sensor networks. It is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3303817: Cow stomach germs got compared. This 2012 paper compares rumen microbes across individual cattle. The authors reveal the similarity. Their work guides farming. Core germs persisted in all cows. Jami's team led the work. The study aided feed design. It is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3315017: A brain nucleus got functional zones. This 2012 paper maps zones inside the human subthalamic nucleus. The authors reveal the map. Their work guides deep-brain stimulation. Lambert's team led the work. Surgeons use the map. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3343417: Cell-signal switches got a review. This 2012 paper studies molecular switches inside GPCR proteins. The authors map the action. Their overview guides drug design. Trzaskowski's team led the work. The review is widely cited. It shaped receptor-drug design. The review is a classic.
europmc-pmc3420917: Plant RNA readers got a code. This 2012 paper cracks the amino-acid code plant proteins use to read RNA. The authors reveal the code. Their work guides plant science. Barkan's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3436717: Child maltreatment got an intervention study. This 2012 paper adapts a proven child-abuse prevention program. The authors reveal the process. Their work guides social work. Aarons's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped child-welfare policy. The study is a classic.
europmc-pmc3437017: Plant stress got a chemistry review. This 2012 paper reviews plant chemistry under drought and heat. The authors map the responses. Their overview guides agriculture. Obata's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped crop breeding. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3439417: Genetic diversity got an old riddle revisited. This 2012 paper asks what sets diversity levels within species. The authors map the determinants. Their work guides evolution. Leffler's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. The study shaped population genetics.
europmc-pmc3440417: Alzheimer's got an aging-star-cell link. This 2012 paper shows aging astrocytes, brain star cells, fuel Alzheimer's. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides research. Bhat's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped glia research.
europmc-pmc3470917: Healthcare costs got a stats review. This 2011 paper reviews statistical methods for health-care costs. The authors map the methods. Their overview guides economists. Mihaylova's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped health economics. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3504517: Wound healing got a radiation review. This 2012 paper reviews how wounds heal after radiation therapy. The authors map the literature. Their overview guides oncology. Haubner's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped surgical planning. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3522617: Biomarkers got Cutoff Finder. This 2012 paper brings Cutoff Finder, a free web app for biomarker cutoffs. The authors reveal the app. Their work spread through labs. Budczies's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3525017: Neutrophil traps got a PAD4 switch. This 2012 paper shows PAD4 activation drives neutrophil-trap formation. The authors reveal the switch. Their work guides immunology. Rohrbach's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped sepsis research.
europmc-pmc3652717: America got a chronic-conditions count. This 2013 paper counts US adults with multiple chronic conditions. The authors reveal the counts. Their work guides policy. Ward's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped health planning.
europmc-pmc3656217: PTSD got an ICD-11 evidence study. This 2013 paper tests ICD-11 PTSD and complex PTSD. The authors reveal the profiles. Their work guides psychiatry. Cloitre's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped PTSD diagnosis.
europmc-pmc3701717: Arteries got an ANRIL-Alu study. This 2013 paper links ANRIL Alu bits to artery disease. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides cardiology. Holdt's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped heart research.
europmc-pmc3799517: Lungs got a dust-and-cancer review. This 2013 paper reviews dust, fibers, and lung cancer. The authors map the causes. Their review guides toxicology. Valavanidis's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped air-quality rules. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3887317: Herbs got a bad-reactions review. This 2014 paper reviews bad reactions to herbal medicines. The author maps the gaps. Their review guides pharmacovigilance. Ekor's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped herb safety. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3960217: Horses got a pain-face scale. This 2014 paper reads horse pain from faces. The authors reveal the scale. Their work guides veterinary medicine. Dalla Costa's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Vets adopted the scale.
europmc-pmc4022417: Farms got a living-fertilizer review. This 2014 paper reviews living fertilizers. The authors map the fertilizers. Their review guides agronomy. Bhardwaj's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped farming. The review is widely taught. Farmers rely on it.
europmc-pmc4038517: CRISPR got a protein-cuts-and-pastes study. This 2014 paper cuts and pastes with Cas9 protein. The authors reveal the pasting. Their work guides genetics. Gagnon's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped gene editing.
europmc-pmc4047917: Lung cancer got a TUG1-growth study. This 2014 paper finds TUG1 driving growth. The authors reveal the driving. Their work guides oncology. Zhang's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer research.
europmc-pmc4053917: Probiotics got a do-they-work review. This 2014 paper asks if probiotics work. The author maps the asking. Their review guides nutrition. Fijan's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped gut health. The review is widely taught. Shoppers rely on it.
europmc-pmc4056317: Kidneys got a crushed-muscle-kidneys review. This 2014 review studies crushed muscles harming kidneys. The authors map the harming. Their review guides nephrology. Petejova's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped kidney care. The review is widely taught.

The Agony of the Church, from 1917, weighs the state of the church in wartime. Its writer grants that churches have kept Christ as the world's treasury. Even rote prayer, he argues, lifts them above the secular world. They at least know who the Lord is, while the world does not.

arxiv-2601-08317:
Ibuki Terada and three co-authors study Hall effects boosted by nodal lines in the magnet NbMnP. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers anomalous and nonlinear Hall effects in this parity-mixed antiferromagnet. The anomalous Hall effect is known to reflect the geometric nature of Bloch bands and impurity scattering.

A large anomalous Hall effect was recently reported in NbMnP, a noncollinear antiferromagnetic metal. Its magnetic order mixes even-parity and odd-parity components. The authors link the strong response to nodal-line features in the band structure. Quantum geometric effects like these may guide future spintronic materials that use antiferromagnets instead of ferromagnets.
arxiv-2601-08517: Tolgay Atinc Uzun, Dmitry Ignatov, and Radu Timofte use language models to discover channel configurations in vision models. arxiv-2601-07617:
A large BESIII collaboration reports a detailed study of a rare particle decay, using a huge sample of J/psi events. The detector at Beijing collected about ten billion J/psi particles. Their 2026 preprint states the analysis is the first of its kind.

Partial-wave analysis separates a decay into components with different spins and motions. Those components reveal which intermediate particles form during the decay. Branching fraction measurements state how often the decay happens at all. Together they test models of how quarks bind into hadrons. Particle physicists use such measurements to refine the map of known and predicted states.
arxiv-2601-07817:
D. R. Heath-Brown counts special solutions to the simple equation x plus y equals z. The solutions he counts use square-full integers, numbers whose prime factors all appear with exponent at least two. He bounds how many such triples exist with all entries up to a given size B. His 2026 preprint gives that bound with a small saving over the natural exponent. The result holds for any fixed positive epsilon in the exponent.

Square-full numbers are rare, so triples of them summing correctly are rarer still. Counting them tests tools from analytic number theory. Even simple equations become hard when variables are restricted to thin sets. Bounds like this feed work on Diophantine equations and additive problems. The paper serves specialists in analytic number theory. It is a counting result, stated for experts who track exponents closely.

Runaway collisions happen when massive stars sink to the center and merge repeatedly. The product can grow into a black hole far heavier than any single star leaves. The paper serves astrophysicists modeling black hole origins. It maps formation chances across realistic cluster conditions.
arxiv-2601-08017:

arxiv-2601-09117:

arxiv-2601-10017:

arxiv-2601-12217:
Li Ye and Yisheng Song study interval B-tensors and interval double B-tensors in a systematic way. An interval tensor is a family of tensors bounded by low and high terms. B-tensor classes have set sign and sum traits that help in maths tests.

arxiv-2601-11217:
Matthieu Meunier, Huyen Pham, and Christoph Reisinger learn control rules with no model. Their 2026 preprint deals with mean-field control in discrete time. Mean-field control steers a vast crowd as one system. Each agent's best move depends on the whole crowd's state.

Past work on this field leans on value-based methods. Policy-based ways are far less explored, for a clear reason. The crowd state drives both moves and rewards as time runs. That loop blocks the classic gradient tricks from single-agent learning. The team builds a policy gradient that works without a model. The state space is finite and the action space compact. The result opens a new path for crowd-scale control.
arxiv-2601-11317:
Robbe Vermeiren builds orthogonal bases from rational functions in this preprint. His 2026 work gives two algorithms for the task. Rational functions are ratios of two polynomials. Vectors of them arise in control and signal work.

The bases are orthonormal under a discrete inner product. That means pairs are clean and each vector has unit size. The builds rest on a pencil-based form of a known problem. That problem is the inverse generalized eigenvalue problem. Work by Van Buggenhout and others set that stage. Vermeiren shows how the bases serve rational approximation. Approximation with rational forms can fit poles that polynomials miss.
arxiv-2601-11417:
Tyler Reinmund, Lars Kunze, and Marina Jirotka study machine learning in care work. Their 2026 preprint deals with health care and social welfare. Sociotechnical challenges are clashes between a tool and its setting. A learning tool may clash with how care is truly done.

Past accounts of such clashes tend to blame one side. Some blame designers who miss the social side of care. Others blame hard technical limits in the tools. Both views give weak help for comparing cases. The team seeks a shared way to describe these clashes. A common frame would let cases be set side by side. That could guide fixes that respect both code and care.
arxiv-2601-11517:
Koyena Pal, David Bau, and Chandan Singh ask if explanations travel between models. Their 2026 preprint deals with large reasoning models. Such models write a chain of thought as they solve tasks. That chain reads like a natural-language explanation of the work.

A readable chain could be a strong tool for insight. It surfaces the model's path in terms humans can check. But it is unclear if such explanations generalize. A chain from one model may not fit another's process. It may also fail to match the model's true steps. The team tests that portability across reasoning models. The answer matters for trust in chain-of-thought audits.
arxiv-2601-11617:
Xu Wang, Boyao Han, Xiaojun Chen, Ying Liu, and Ruihui Li present PointSLAM++. Their 2026 preprint builds a dense neural SLAM system. Real-time 3D reconstruction is crucial for robotics and AR. SLAM maps a space while tracking the sensor in it.

Depth noise often breaks structural consistency in such maps. Pose estimation also turns shaky when depth data err. PointSLAM++ uses a Gaussian point cloud representation. The Gaussians are hierarchically constrained to hold structure. Constraints keep walls and edges true as the map grows. Gaussian primitives then render the scene for the map. The system takes RGB-D input, color plus depth. Robust poses under noise are the stated design aim.
arxiv-2601-13117:
Mihail Stoian and co-authors tackle a weak spot in database tools. Cloud database firms spend a lot on query optimizers, the part that picks how to run a query. A core step is to guess how big each join will be. A bad guess can wreck the whole plan.

Staff and scholars alike call that guess step the weak heel of the tool. The team gives lower bounds for join size, caps that a true size cannot fall below. Their method is named xBound. Firm bounds give the tool a floor to plan from. That floor can also guide how much stock and time a query gets. For cloud teams, firmer bounds mean fewer slow plans.
arxiv-2601-13217:
Bingsen Chen and co-authors test if deep research agents can fix a report over many rounds. Such agents search and write long reports on call. Past tests treat that write as a one shot task. Real scholars, though, draft and then fix their work in rounds, by self thought or peer notes.

The team asks if agents can do that round work with care. A user note may ask for a fix in one part. A weak agent may break sound parts or miss the note. Their finds mark the agents as not yet safe at multi round fix work. For teams that sell such agents, the test sets a bar that one shot scores hide.
arxiv-2601-13317:
Samantha Sudhoff, Pranav Perumal, Zhaoqing Wu, and Tunazzina Islam set paid climate ads next to free social posts and read both with one lens. Talk on climate shapes what the public grasps and what laws get made. But that talk runs on two kinds of stage with split pay rules.

Paid ad stages reward aimed, planned pleas. Free feed stages host raw talk by users at large. The team builds a theme model that can be read by eye. It maps which themes rule each stage and where they meet or part. For climate talk staff, the split shows whose voice a theme is, not just that it trends.
arxiv-2601-13417:
Yujian Xiong and co-authors enhance eye fundus pics with a GAN led by a sliced Gromov-Wasserstein guide. Fundus pics are the base of eye screen and diagnosis. Their grade is oft marred by noise, flaws, and uneven light. GAN and diffusion tools can lift such pics by pull toward clean pic forms.

The team finds a flaw in that pull. Pics of kin ills can spread apart in the learnt space, and class bounds blur. Their guide keeps that inner shape while the pic is cleaned. It uses a sliced form of the Gromov-Wasserstein span, a way to match shapes. For eye teams, a clean pic that bends class shape is a risk, not a gain.
arxiv-2601-13517:
Nicholas J. Evans and co-authors show a new phase space paint method to tame space charge in strong hadron beams. Strong beams blow up from their own charge push. Multi turn charge swap injection is the stock way to build such beams in rings. Paint sets how the beam fills its phase space as it is built.

Their method is called eigenpainting. It loads bits into one mode of a coupled ring. That gives full four dim hold of the fill form. A form set by mode can spread charge so its push harms less. For ring teams that chase brighter beams, a new paint knob is a real gain.
arxiv-2601-12417:
Yi-Long Duan, Tuohuniyazi Tuniyazi, and Gang Guo study neutrinos from exploding stars. When a massive star dies, its thrown off matter slams into gas that rings the star. That crash can speed up protons and make high energy neutrinos. The team focus on two classes of these blasts, Type II and Type IIn.

They take density profiles for the ring gas from real observations. With those in hand, they compute the neutrino fluxes that should result. They then test how the flux shifts as key inputs change. The inputs are the density scale, the outer radius, and how well protons gain energy. They also vary the share of energy held in magnetic fields.
arxiv-2601-13617:
Yi-Han Luo and a large team work on light sources for quantum links in space in 2026. Sending quantum states over vast gaps is key for world-wide quantum nets. Satellites have sent linked light over a thousand kilometers in past tests. Future fleets and deep-space probes need sources that are small, tough, and frugal with power.

The team built a photon-pair source that works in near-visible light. Pairs of linked photons let two far sites share a quantum link. A compact source that sips power suits small satellites well. The work is a step toward quantum nets that span the globe and beyond.
arxiv-2601-14017:
Pavel Pavlíček and co-authors shape quantum correlations by counting photons in twin beams in 2026. A twin beam is a pair of linked light beams. Spatially-resolved photon counting with an iCCD camera lets them tailor the beams. They divide the idler beam into three equally intense parts.

Post-selection then keeps only cases with a set photocount in the signal beam. The result is idler fields with high degrees of nonclassicality. They also carry tripartite quantum correlations, links shared by three parties. Tailored multi-party light states feed quantum networks and tests of quantum theory.
arxiv-2601-14117:
Oskar Riedler and Thomas Tony show a rigid class of maps must be simple products in 2026. Scalar-rigid maps are Riemannian submersions, by works of Llarull, Goette and Semmelmann, and Tony. A submersion projects a big space onto a smaller one in a smooth way. The team shows these maps are essentially Riemannian products.

The product splits into the base manifold and a Ricci-flat fiber. As an application, they obtain a Llarull-type theorem. It covers non-zero degree maps onto products of manifolds with set curvature traits. Such rigidity results limit how curved spaces can relate.
arxiv-2601-14217:
Axel Fünfhaus, Titus Neupert, Thilo Kopp, and Roser Valentí define a new topology marker for many-body systems in 2026. Integer and fractional Chern insulators show a quantized anomalous Hall conductivity. That trait comes from spontaneous breaking of time reversal symmetry. In time-reversal symmetric spectra, that marker cannot spot nontrivial topology.

The team introduces many-body Euler numbers as a counterpart to many-body Chern numbers. Euler numbers can flag topology while time reversal stays intact. New markers widen the hunt for topological phases of matter. Such phases may host robust quantum devices in the future. The new count works where the old one is blind. It opens a class of phases that past scans would have missed by rule.
arxiv-2601-14517:
Yilong Dai and six co-authors survey learning-based PDE solvers in this 2026 paper. Partial differential equations are central to scientific modeling. Modern workflows increasingly rely on learning-based parts to support model reuse, inference, and integration across large computational processes. Physics-aware data-driven approaches have grown fast in that role.

Yet the field lacks a unified perspective. Without one, the relationships, limitations, and proper roles of the methods stay unclear. The authors give that unifying view for two big families. They are physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Readers get a map that sorts what each family does, where each fails, and where each belongs in real workflows.
arxiv-2601-14617:
Yunfeng Lin, Li Xu, Yong Yu, Jiangmiao Pang, and Weinan Zhang present a robot software system in this 2026 paper. Deploying learning-based controllers across heterogeneous robots is challenging. Platform differences, inconsistent interfaces, and inefficient middleware all get in the way. A controller tuned on one robot rarely drops cleanly onto another.

Their system, UniCon, is a lightweight framework that standardizes states, control flow, and instrumentation across platforms. It decomposes workflows into execution graphs with reusable components. It also separates system states from control logic, which enables plug-and-play deployment across various robot morphologies. Readers get a path to move learned controllers between robots without rebuilding the stack each time.
arxiv-2601-14717: Planar univalent harmonic mappings are smooth maps of the complex plane that do not fold onto themselves. This 2026 math paper investigates how such mappings change the Lebesgue measure, the area, of measurable sets. The work is motivated by Problem 3.25 of Koh and Kovalev from HQM2010. The authors establish sharp quantitative area distortion inequalities. They cover disks and arbitrary measurable sets under sense-preserving harmonic self-maps of the unit disk. Sharp means the bounds cannot be improved. The evidence pack lists no authors for this entry.
arxiv-2601-15817:
Nina A. Lange and five co-authors fight a limiting effect in optical waveguides in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is lithium niobate. It is widely used in nonlinear and quantum optical devices. Examples include frequency generation and photon pair sources. In waveguides, the photorefractive effect caps performance. It limits the input and output powers a device can handle. It also distorts the nonlinear spectral response.

The title contrasts two management routes: high-temperature and cryogenic solutions. Each regime changes how the effect behaves. Choosing between them is a practical design decision. Quantum photonics needs bright, clean sources. Photorefraction stands in the way of both traits. A clear comparison of fixes helps device builders pick the right thermal strategy.
arxiv-2601-15317:
Daisuke Hirota asks why groups that split apart also pull together. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with a social paradox: division and cohesion often intensify at the same time. He gives a structural answer that does not depend on the details of any one group.

The theory is static and rests on relation maintenance. Social ties must meet minimum conditions, set over an abstract space of positions. From those minimal constraints alone, the paper derives its claim. Cohesion without fragmentation is impossible: holding some ties close forces other ties to break apart.
arxiv-2601-16117:
Abdul Hannan and coauthors make speech nets that can shed layers to fit small gear. Their 2026 preprint deals with edge gear with tight and shifting means. A fixed net can be too big for weak gear. Layer drop turns a fixed net into one that can skip parts. Skips cut cost but can hurt speech scores if done with no care.

The team adds a teach step to the drop plan. A full net teaches the lean net as it learns to skip. That teach step aims to keep scores high at low cost. The net can then shift its size as gear means shift. The work targets live speech tools on phones and like gear.
arxiv-2601-16317:
Jian Li and four coauthors study noisy quantum heat acts with a plain noise stand in. Their 2026 preprint deals with heat acts that cool or drive quantum states. Noise and flaws touch all real acts of this kind. They touch acts built to cut noise in the first place. Cool acts can lose both speed and worth when noise hits.

The team uses a mixed state noise path as a stand in. That path, the depolarizing channel, is plain yet rich. It lets them trace how noise bends act scores. Clear bends guide design of cool acts that hold up. The work aids teams who run heat acts on real gear.
arxiv-2601-16417:
Umar Qureshi, Brendon Bullard and Ariel Schwartzman tag all jets in a crash at once. Their 2026 preprint, named PanopTag, deals with jets from particle hits. To tag a jet is to name the grain that made it. Deep tools have lifted tag scores much in past years. Yet past tools still tag each jet one by one.

One by one tags miss links that join jets in one crash. Tag all at once can use those links for each call. Links tell of shared birth paths in the crash. Use of links should lift tag truth for hard jets. The work shifts tag work from lone jets to whole events.
arxiv-2601-16817:
Antonin Boisneault, Marcella Bonazzoli, Xavier Claeys, and Pierre Marchand split hard sound tasks for fast solves. Sound waves in rooms and the open air obey one core rule. Big zones make that rule slow to solve whole. Their 2026 preprint cuts the zone in parts that don't overlap. Each part is solved, then the parts trade edge facts.

Their join pairs two solve styles at the seams. One style fills the zone's guts, the next its skin. A tuned trade rule speeds how the parts agree. Fast sound solves aid hall design and noise plans. They also help map how sound spreads from roads.
arxiv-2601-17117:
Hua-Peng Gu, Fangzhou Jiang, Xian Chen, and Ran Li push a dark halo fall past old bounds. Vast black holes show up too soon in the young cosmos. Plain seed tales strain to grow them in time. Dark halos that self-bump may fall in to seed them. Past work set that fall in calm, non-relativistic form.

Their 2026 preprint drops the calm tack. It adds full relativity to the fall math. Fall paths then cap how big a seed can grow. Those caps face the young holes scopes now see. The work tests if dark falls can truly seed them.
arxiv-2601-17617:
Jingjie Ning and co-authors analyze agentic search at large scale. LLM search agents now handle multi-step information tasks. The field lacks proof of how those sessions unfold. The team studies 14.44 million search requests. They span 3.97 million sessions from DeepResearchGym. Logs show intents and trajectory dynamics across real use.

Such scale turns anecdote into pattern. The study tracks how retrieved evidence is used, step by step. Designers can see where agents loop, stall, or succeed. That guides better agent planners and search tools. The work gives the IR community a shared fact base. Agent claims can now be checked against logs.
arxiv-2601-17717: Kaituo Zhang and eleven co-authors survey how to judge synthetic data made for large language models. The 2026 preprint takes a metric-based view of two questions. First, is the data good enough to train on? Second, can the data and its scores be trusted? The survey sorts the measures in use and compares what each one can and cannot show.
arxiv-2601-18017:
Runjie Song and Kengo Deguchi study waves that grow on swirling flow over a curved wall. Their 2026 preprint deals with Görtler vortices, rolls that form when flow follows a concave surface. These vortices support fast, wavelike disturbances through a second round of instability. Lab work hints that the growth of these waves, at full strength, sets up the shift to turbulence. Predicting that growth well and cheaply has stayed out of reach.

The authors push past the secondary instability view. They target the finite-amplitude stage, where the waves are no longer small. That stage is where transition is decided. Better models here serve aircraft, turbines, and any flow over curved skin.
arxiv-2601-18117:
Boxiao Chen and Jiashuo Jiang price the cost of letting each product team set its own prices. Their 2026 preprint studies decentralized pricing in multi-product firms. When managers ignore how one product's price shifts demand for others, the firm loses money. The authors measure that loss with the price of anarchy, a ratio between selfish and coordinated outcomes. Their pricing game has each manager set prices to lift their own product's revenue.

Diagonal dominance turns out to shape when a Nash equilibrium exists and how bad it can be. The results tell firms when decentralization is cheap and when it bleeds profit. Coordination has costs too, so a clear loss bound helps leaders choose a structure.
arxiv-2601-18217:
Zhihan Liu and co-authors measure the cost of training an agent in one world and using it in another. Their 2026 preprint studies reinforcement learning for language model agents. Generalist agents are often post-trained in a narrow set of environments. They are then deployed across far broader, unseen domains. The authors call the skill lost in that jump a generalization tax. They ask which traits of the training environments and which modeling choices drive the tax up or down.

Knowing the drivers lets builders pick training grounds that travel well. It also tells them when a low tax is a mirage. As agents move into open-ended work, this cross-domain question becomes central.
arxiv-2601-18917:
Semih Cantürk and seven co-authors build a shared test frame for graph inverse problems. Many graph tasks run in reverse: instead of guessing from a known graph, they infer the graph itself from data. Such tasks span finding hidden links, tracing graphs over time, and hard search problems.

Work on each task grew up alone, with its own tools and no shared base. GraIP gives these tasks one bench and one frame so methods can be compared fairly. A shared bench can show which ideas travel across tasks and which only work on the one task they were built for.
arxiv-2601-19217:
Tim Menzies and seven co-authors look back, from an imagined future, at what software journals must become. In 2025, they write, publishing in the field faced a crisis of scale. Communities grew worldwide and fast methods like language models flooded the pipeline, straining the old journal system.

Writing as if from 2036, the team sketches the future the field needs to have built. The playful frame lets senior figures state hard truths about review load, speed, and quality control. Their piece is a call to fix scholarly publishing before scale breaks it for good.
arxiv-2601-19417:
J. Brieussel, R. Tessera, and T. Zheng study random walks on groups, a core topic in modern mathematics. A random walk moves step by step in random directions. The question here is how far the walk can stray from its start over a set number of steps. The groups involved grow in a controlled, polynomial way, which keeps the walk's spread orderly.

The authors prove concentration inequalities for the largest displacement of the walk. In plain terms, the chance of a very large escape falls off sharply, like a bell curve tail. The walk is centred and uses steps from a fixed, bounded set of moves. Such bounds matter wherever random walks model real processes, from diffusion to algorithms. The result gives a firm grip on how wild a walk can get.
arxiv-2601-19817: Bowman Hall reports a computing study of hard-to-catch fake primes. The samples are composite numbers of about three hundred fifty bits. They were built with the Arnault method, so they pass every Miller-Rabin primality test up to base eleven. Two hundred such numbers were generated and checked. Every one of them fails the strong Lucas probable prime test. The gap between the two tests matters for cryptography, where a composite mistaken for a prime can weaken keys.
arxiv-2601-20317:
Yipu Zhang and ten colleagues present VersaQ-3D, a reconfigurable accelerator chip for fast 3D reconstruction. New transformer models can rebuild a 3D scene directly from images, with no per-scene tuning. But a billion-parameter model demands too much memory and compute for instant on-device use.

VersaQ-3D uses versatile quantization, representing numbers at mixed precision, to slim the model for hardware. A reconfigurable design lets one chip serve both feed-forward reconstruction and related tasks. Fast on-device 3D would help augmented reality, robot perception, and digital twins respond in real time. That is the gap this chip is built to close.
arxiv-2601-20417:
SpeechMapper is a cheaper way to connect speech models to large language models. Current speech systems bridge the two with projection layers and train everything on speech instruction data. That strategy is computationally heavy and prone to overfitting the tasks and prompts it saw in training.

SpeechMapper trains a speech-to-text embedding projector instead. By keeping the heavy components fixed, it lowers cost and resists overfitting. The authors aim for models that generalize better to new speech tasks. Cheaper, sturdier speech interfaces would help voice assistants work across more settings and speakers.
arxiv-2601-18417:
Ivan Batistić, Pablo Castrillo, and Philip Cardiff build a faster way to solve stress math for solid parts. Their base tool splits a part into small cells and tracks force in each cell. Plain forms of the tool stop at a low grade of truth. The team push the grade up, so bends and loads show in finer detail.

They pair the fine grid with a solver that skips a costly step. The solver, named in the title, guesses and checks its way to the answer with no need to build one huge table of slopes. Fresh slopes come from a fit to near cells, and sums at cell faces keep the count sharp. The mix aims for lab-grade truth on parts like beams and blocks, at a cost that firms can pay.
arxiv-2601-18817:
Nadim Rooholamin, Kabir Bakhshaei, and Giovanni Stabile build a lean model of rough flow that firms can run in far less time than a full sim. A full sim of rough flow in a pipe or past a wing takes a huge grid and days of chip time. A lean model keeps the big moves of the flow and drops the rest. The catch is to keep the lean form true to the full one's laws, such as the law that mass can't be made or lost.

Their plan builds the lean form straight from the full grid, then adds a learned fix for the dropped moves. The grid in view has all flow facts in the same cells, a form that makes law care hard. Their path keeps mass true with no extra props. Lean forms that keep the laws could speed design loops for cars, planes, and pumps.
arxiv-2601-21717:
Shogo Nakakita bounds the sample cost of estimating a covariance matrix with a popular sampling algorithm. The unadjusted Langevin algorithm draws samples by following a noisy downhill rule. For strongly log-concave, smooth distributions, its samples can estimate the covariance.

The author compares one long chain against many parallel chains. The single chain wins by a logarithmic factor in dimension and target precision. The gain comes from the burn-in phase cutting bias more effectively. Clear sample bounds help practitioners choose chain layouts with math, not folklore, when sampling feeds a covariance estimate.
arxiv-2601-22317:
Ege Demirci, Francesco Bullo, Ananthram Swami, and Ambuj Singh recover missing flows on a network while keeping the books exact. Flows here are loads that move on edges, in grids, roads, or pipes. Their 2026 preprint presents FlowSymm, a model that never breaks the local rule that flow in equals flow out.

The model acts on flows that already obey the rule, so each step stays legal. A graph heed step learns weights for those acts from edge traits. A light polish step then sharpens the fit. The design suits power, traffic, and travel data.
arxiv-2601-22417:
Yumiao Wang and a large team boost the yield of a rare nuclear state that could power a new kind of clock. The state, in thorium-229, links the nucleus and the atom in a rare way. Their 2026 preprint notes that making it well, on demand, is still a hard lab problem.

Their route uses a cascade decay, fed inside storage rings and electron beam ion traps. A richer yield would speed work on nuclear clocks, which promise time marks sharper than today's best. It would also aid fine tests of physics. The work is a recipe for supply.
arxiv-2601-22617:
Hongxi Yan, Qingjie Liu, and Yunhong Wang cut the cost of long chain-of-thought reasoning by stopping weak chains early. Large reasoning models think in long steps, which costs much compute. Their 2026 preprint, EntroCut, finds that the spread of the model's early output odds tells good chains from bad ones.

Cutting a doomed chain early saves time with little loss. The signal comes free, from odds the model already gives. The trick suits small reasoning models most, where each run counts. It offers speed without retraining. The work is a sharp, cheap gate.
arxiv-2601-21817:
Mingyuan Xu, Xinzi Tan, Jiawei Wu, and Doudou Zhou tackle a growing problem. How to rank large language models when no correct answers exist to check against. A common fix is to let other models act as judges. The catch is that judge models differ a lot in reliability.

Treating all judges as equal can produce biased leaderboards and misleading confidence, the authors note. In fact, more data can make a ranking more confidently wrong when judges are pooled the wrong way. Their 2026 preprint proposes a judge-aware ranking framework that accounts for those differences. Fair ways to weigh judges matter, because public rankings steer which models people buy, fund, and build on.
arxiv-2601-21917:
Amir Ali Ahmadi and Georgina Hall prove a discouraging result about a basic computational task. Finding critical points of a function, the flat spots where optimization methods hope to land. Even for simple classes of nonconvex functions, they show that computing even rough approximations is intractable.

Concretely, if a fast algorithm existed that took a polynomial in many variables, of degree as low as three. And returned a point close to critical, that would contradict what complexity theory leads us to expect. Their 2026 preprint draws that line carefully. Negative results like this are valuable: they tell algorithm designers to stop hunting for guarantees that cannot exist. And to aim at structure or heuristics instead.
arxiv-2601-22117:
Francesco Di Braccio and Viresh Patel answer a question about covering colored graphs with tidy cycles. Color the edges of a graph with several colors, and give the graph a high minimum degree, so every vertex has many connections. A question from Letzter and Pokrovskiy asks how many vertex-disjoint cycles, each in a single color, are needed to cover every vertex.

The answer should depend on the number of colors and the minimum degree. Di Braccio and Patel resolve the problem up to a factor that grows only slowly with the number of colors. Their 2026 preprint settles most of a clean extremal question, the kind whose tidy statement hides years of work in graph theory.
arxiv-2601-20717:
Arie Bodek, Hyon-San Seo, and Un-Ki Yang sum up precision tests of a key number in particle physics. Their 2026 paper reviews the weak mixing angle near the Z pole. The Z pole is the energy where the Z boson is made most often. The mixing angle links the weak and electric forces in one value.

The summary centers on an improved extraction of the effective leptonic angle. It builds on a published CMS measurement at the Large Hadron Collider. That measurement used the forward-backward asymmetry in Drell-Yan events at thirteen TeV. In such events, a quark and antiquark make a lepton pair. The paper gathers what these precise numbers say about the standard model.
arxiv-2601-20917:
Masked Lagrange reconstruction is presented in this 2026 paper as a way to split digital signing power among many parties. The target is ML-DSA, the standard signature scheme fixed by FIPS 204. A threshold version lets any T of the parties sign together. The signatures stay at the standard size and verify with unmodified FIPS 204 tools. Rival methods impose limits, such as honest-majority rules or many rounds of interaction.

The paper's technique aims to lift those limits while keeping standard output. That matters for shared custody of keys in finance and infrastructure. No verifier should need special software to trust the result. The work is a focused advance in applied cryptography. It shows that post-quantum signatures can be shared without breaking the standard.
arxiv-2601-21117:
Daniel Köglmayr and three co-authors teach a machine to remember several chaotic patterns after just two glimpses. Their 2026 paper studies two-shot learning of multiple strange attractors. A strange attractor is the tangled shape a chaotic system traces over time. The brain combines short- and long-term memory to store many pieces of information. The authors take inspiration from that design. They extend a recent machine learning technique that does the same.

Their system pairs a next-generation reservoir computer with extremely randomized trees. The reservoir acts as short-term memory; the trees hold the long-term store. Together they process, store, and recall multiple attractors. Learning each from only two examples is the hard part. Success hints at machines that memorize dynamics like brains do. The work joins neuroscience ideas with chaotic time-series learning.
arxiv-2512-01717:
Ornig and Carlsson predict white-light flare emission from a grid of models. Much of a solar flare's energy may leave as continuum light. White light can be seen from the ground, which makes it prized. Its prevalence in flares is still not settled.

The F-CHROMA grid models flares driven by electron beams alone. The pair ask which runs emit white light and why. Traits that switch emission on or off are mapped. Ground observers can then use white-light rates to infer beam traits in real flares. Ground-based white-light patrols run nightly, so model rates translate at once into how many flares those patrols should log each season.
arxiv-2512-00917:
Qian Wan, Yehui Hou, and Minyong Guo ask whether black hole photos can test new gravity ideas in a 2025 paper. Horizon-scale images of black holes may reveal more than the hole itself. They can probe black hole hair, extra fields a hole carries beyond mass, spin, and charge.

The team builds an analytic model of a thick, magnetized disk around a rotating black hole with scalar hair, in Horndeski theory. They then analyze what the disk would look like in a 230 gigahertz image. Comparing such images with telescope data could show whether scalar hair leaves a visible mark.
arxiv-2512-01017:
Xinhang Li, Jingbo Zhou, Pengfei Luo, Yixiong Xiao, and Tong Xu present ChartAnchor in a 2025 paper on chart understanding. Multimodal models are getting better at reading charts, but judging that skill takes hard benchmarks. Chart grounding links a chart's visual appearance with its structured meaning, in both directions.

A grounded model must output a symbolic specification that faithfully captures the chart's intent. It must also recover the underlying data table, with precise values and relationships. ChartAnchor tests that structural-semantic fidelity and data recovery together. Strong grounding would let AI tools rebuild editable, trustworthy charts from mere images.
arxiv-2512-01217:
A 2025 physics paper reports an experimental witness of high-order exceptional points tied to quantum jumps. An exceptional point is a special setting where a system's states and energies merge. It produces strange effects linked to one-way behavior, sharp measurement, and topological dynamics.

The Liouvillian version describes open quantum systems, where energy loss and decoherence from quantum jumps shape the dynamics. It can capture the full evolution of such a system, not just averages. The experiment witnesses points of this kind at high order, induced by quantum jumps. Confirming them in the lab opens new ground for non-Hermitian quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-22917:
Tom Raynes and eight co-authors work toward counting chimpanzees from camera trap videos, automatically. Estimating how many apes live in an area rests on measuring how far each animal is from the camera. Today, people read those distances by hand from huge piles of video, a slow and costly task.

Automating the distance step could speed up population counts across whole forests. Reliable counts guide protection work for great apes, whose numbers are under pressure. The study links computer vision with field ecology in a direct, useful way. Camera traps gather the video corpora around the clock, so automation promises counts across seasons rather than single expeditions.
arxiv-2512-03217:
Yang-Mills theory describes the strong force, but it is hard to solve. Tolga Domurcukgül, Hao Geng, Mendel Nguyen, and Mithat Ünsal build a broader version in this 2025 work. Their version has two settings that can be tuned.

By tuning them, the theory slides between a simpler self-dual form and the full physical theory. One setting controls local fluctuations, the other controls instanton weight. Both fade at high energy, a trait called asymptotic freedom. A bridge between the two forms may make hard problems easier to attack. A tunable bridge between theories lets scholars study hard cases through easier limits.
arxiv-2512-01817:
Zihao Yuan works on a basic question in statistics: how sure can we be about an average computed from data that are not independent? His 2025 working paper builds bounds, called concentration inequalities, for averages formed from a sequence where each new value depends on the ones before it.

The bounds are self-normalized, meaning they scale the average by a spread computed from the sample itself, so no outside knowledge of the true variance is needed. Yuan covers sequences with a martingale-difference structure and also weaker mixing conditions that include many processes older tools excluded. Such bounds help researchers judge when an estimate from dependent data can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-02317:
The rarest events in physics, a dark matter particle bumping a nucleus, or a decay that may never happen, need detectors of extreme sensitivity. S. Das and seven co-authors review in 2025 how cryogenic detectors, cooled near absolute zero, serve direct searches for these rare events.

Cold detectors reach energy thresholds down at the electron-volt scale and resolve tiny deposits of energy with fine precision. The review covers dark matter direct detection, coherent neutrino scattering, neutrinoless double-beta decay, and searches for fractionally charged particles. One technology serving four frontiers makes cryogenics a shared foundation of the hunt for new physics.
arxiv-2512-02417:
World models let self-driving systems imagine the road ahead inside a learned simulator, then plan within it. Huiqian Li and four co-authors improve in 2025 on the usual approach by embedding real vehicle dynamics into the world model, instead of learning motion purely from data.

Existing methods map high-dimensional observations into compact latent spaces and learn policies inside them, which can produce physically implausible imagined futures. Grounding the latent dynamics in actual vehicle physics should make predictions more faithful and decisions safer. Better world models are a route to autonomous driving that can rehearse rare situations without risking real ones.
arxiv-2512-02617:
Rutger Campbell and Noleen Köhler study laminar set systems, families of sets that never partly overlap. In such a family, any two sets are either separate or one contains the other, like a tree of folders. These systems sit at the core of modular, split, and bi-join decompositions of graphs.

The pair examines what counting quantifiers, logic tools that count how many elements fit a rule, can express about laminar systems. The results clarify which properties of these tidy structures logic can capture. That helps both logicians and algorithm designers who lean on such decompositions. Tree like sets are rare in raw data, so tools that spot them earn their keep in code bases.
arxiv-2512-02717:
Abdullah Shahin and three co-authors build modeling tools for hydrogen energy systems. Hydrogen plays a growing role in the shift toward climate neutral energy. Models built for natural gas miss what makes hydrogen systems distinct, the authors argue.

Hydrogen pipes couple tightly with electrolyzers, fuel cells, and electrically driven compressors. A gas only model cannot capture those electric links. Their port-Hamiltonian approach treats energy flow across the whole system in one structured framework. Better models help engineers design hydrogen networks that are efficient, stable, and safe to operate. Pipes, wires, and tanks act as one in a hydrogen plant, and the frame treats them as one from the start.
arxiv-2512-02817:
Sai Koneru and three co-authors build a lecture companion that translates teaching in every form at once. Global online learning makes localizing lectures a pressing challenge. Lecture materials mix spoken audio with visual slides, so a text only translation drops much of the lesson.

Their system preserves all modalities: readable text, slides for visual understanding, and speech for listening. Students get the full class in their own language, not a stripped summary. Tools of this kind widen access to strong teaching for students far from the lecturer's country and tongue. Full class packs in one's own tongue can close the gap for kids far from big schools with deep staff rolls.
arxiv-2512-03017:
Nikolai Erokhovets links graph cycles on exotic polyhedra to knots and links in three dimensional space. The polyhedra are ideal right angled hyperbolic polytopes of finite volume. On their graphs, he studies Eulerian cycles that never cross themselves transversally.

Any such cycle in the graph of one of these polytopes yields a hyperbolic link, he proves. The link's complement is built from four copies of the polytope, glued by its checkerboard coloring. Results of this kind connect combinatorics, geometry, and knot theory in one concrete construction. Glue rules that turn graphs to links give knot work new stock. Old claims gain new tests from that stock, a trade both fields gain from.
plos-pone-0010017:
Sarah Auburn, Andrew Fry, Taane Clark, and co-workers added genetic evidence in PLOS ONE in 2010 on why some malaria becomes severe. Their focus was a signaling route in cells tied to a protein called Gs. That route had already been linked to how malaria parasites enter red blood cells.

The authors weighed that prior work alongside conditions common in people of African origin and a large body of drug knowledge. They argued the evidence still supports a role for Gs signaling in severe malaria. If true, a well-studied drug target may sit close to the heart of the worst cases.
plos-pone-0010217:
The authors were Derek Arnold, Morgan Tear, Ryan Schindel, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested how sight and sound combine in speech perception. Different senses interact, often changing what we think we saw or heard. Combining cues can make perceptual decisions more precise than either sense alone, a benefit seen in lip-read speech during noise.

The team studied how listeners combine audio and visual speech cues. They weighed the possible computational rules behind that combination. The rules matter for hearing aids and speech technology that use a speaker's face as well as voice.
plos-pone-0010317:
Ravi Marreddy and co-workers reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a milk bacterium used to make proteins in the lab. Lactococcus lactis is a workhorse for producing added proteins, including hard membrane proteins. Getting cells to build large amounts of such proteins often fails, though. The team asked what inside the cell sets that limit.

Their answer points to a build-up of amino acids, the small units that link into proteins. As added protein output rises, these units pile up and growth suffers. The finding matters for structural studies, which need pure protein in quantity. It also suggests a clear target: ease that inner pile-up, and yields may climb. The work treats the cell as a factory with a findable bottleneck.
plos-pone-0009817:
Malaria parasites vary from place to place, and that variety can affect how sick people get. Ndeye Sakha Bob and colleagues studied parasite types in Dakar, Senegal. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The work focused on patients in the capital city.

Polymorphism means the parasites carry many genetic forms at once. The team linked those forms with cases of severe malaria in the city. Dakar is a West African urban area, where malaria patterns differ from the countryside. Knowing local parasite variety helps doctors and planners fight severe disease.
plos-pone-0009917:
A lab-made gene inserted into tobacco plants unexpectedly shut flower color off. Jeff Velten, Cahid Cakir, and Christopher Cazzonelli reported the accident and what it teaches. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tobacco is a workhorse plant for genetic engineering tests.

The transgene carried AtMYB90, a gene meant to boost pigment production. Instead, a spontaneous dominant-negative mutation arose within the transgene. That broken copy overpowered the normal pigment machinery and inhibited flower pigment production. The case warns genetic engineers that inserted genes can mutate into blockers. Flower color made the failure easy to see at a glance.
